The simulation of complex quantum systems through time-dependent quantum Monte Carlo methods is hindered by the dimensionality of the problem. A novel approach employs two-layer neural networks to approximate the Schrödinger equation, but this approach has a significant limitation: it only works for systems that have fewer than 40-50 degrees of freedom. We examine how the neural network's inability to generalize well to new dimensions affects its performance, and find that the network's performance declines rapidly as the dimensionality increases beyond its initial limits. The network's inability to generalize is caused by its reliance on the interaction between the input and hidden layers, which leads to overfitting. Our findings suggest that pre-training the network on lower-dimensional systems could improve its performance, but fully understanding the network's generalization abilities will require further research. Ultimately, we conclude that the neural network approach is unlikely to be useful for simulating complex quantum systems. We suggest the use of orthogonal transformations to simplify the high-dimensional problems, and propose a new method based on the Zassenhaus formula to efficiently iterate the exponential operator in the Schrödinger equation. The new method preserves the network's efficiency and offers significant improvements in its performance. The method will be further tested for coming-of-age calculations in our forthcoming work. The research presents a novel approach to approximately finding Schrödinger equation's eigenvalues, and the method's limitations and potential enhancements to the networks are investigated. The study concludes by outlining a future research to efficiently tackle high-dimensional problems in quantum chemistry simulations. Over the past decade, Tumor Infiltrating Lymphocytes (TIL) have emerged as a critical factor in understanding cancer pathology and improving survival rates. Pathologists manually assess TILs using a scale from none to high, but this measurement lacks reliability. A more accurate method involves extracting TIL categories from Whole Slide Images (WSIs), a type of digital microscopy image, which can be automated using deep learning techniques. However, training and testing these models on large WSI collections is impractical due to their massive sizes, requiring or rendering models unsuitable for general use. This problem can be overcome by using Federated Learning (FL) to train models locally on users' devices, but implementing FL on WSI categorization has been challenging. Our work addresses this challenge by developing a novel FL framework for training models on TIL categories, which includes creating a benchmark dataset, designing an optimized training process, and demonstrating superior performance compared to conventional training methods using benchmark and real-world datasets. Our results show that our FL approach achieves the best accuracy when tested on three different datasets, matching or outperforming the performance of models trained on complete datasets, while also respecting data privacy by preventing data transmission. This work will be made available in its entirety to the scientific community, enabling researchers to replicate our results and further improve this approach. Our FL implementation, as well as associated data and models, can be accessed via our GitHub repository. Our work has two primary contributions: establishing a benchmark for training deep learning models to categorize TILs using FL, as well as introducing an efficient training process to overcome the challenges of training on multiple large WSIs. Our findings show that our training process offers excellent performance, serving as a valuable resource for developers looking to apply FL to similar problems, and potentially extending its use to other tumor assessment tasks. Our work has two key outcomes: first, evaluating the efficiency of training models to categorize TILs using FL, and second, introducing an optimized training process to achieve this goal. Satellite imagery plays a vital role in understanding and tracking global environmental changes.
However, analyzing this imagery is extremely computationally expensive and time-consuming.
Due to the size and resolution of the images, they cannot be processed in real-time on standard computers or cloud platforms.
As a result, there is a significant gap between the data generated by satellites and the data needed for meaningful analysis.
To overcome this limitation, we introduce EarthNets, a distributed AI network designed specifically for processing satellite imagery of large geographic areas.
By utilizing a significant amount of GPU memory, EarthNets allows teams to work on projects that were previously infeasible, enabling the analysis of images that cannot be processed on standard GPUs or clouds due to their high resolution and size. 
For example, projects involving the analysis of entire countries or multiple cities require an unprecedented amount of memory, exceeding the capacity of even the largest available GPUs.
By scaling across multiple machines, EarthNets can process images that have sizes and resolutions of 100 GB or more, enabling teams to explore new areas in planet monitoring and surveillance that were previously inaccessible. 
As proof-of-conconcept, we use EarthNets to monitor deforestation and detect signs of slavery in satellite images. 
Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of EarthNets in enabling teams to analyze large geographic areas and highlights the significant memory requirements of these projects. 
As a flexible and general-purpose solution, EarthNets has the potential to revolutionize planet monitoring and surveillance, enabling teams to explore new applications and use cases that were previously infeasible. 
Our future work will focus on scaling across multiple machines and distributed environments. 
In this paper, we present EarthNets as a powerful tool for enabling AI projects that require large-scale geometric data and demonstrate its capabilities with two real-world use cases. Leveraging parallel processing across multiple GPUs, EarthNets can efficiently handle projects and outperform alternative solutions by a significant margin. Our results showcase the memory efficiency and computational speed of EarthNets, underscoring its value as a pioneering solution for large-scale geographic data. A robust method for performing a vibrantly colored renormalization group analysis in high dimensions has been developed, which exactly matches known results for the three-dimensional case. This novel approach can be applied to study other complex systems, such as homeotropic active nematics and two-dimensional active sheets. By analyzing data from galaxies at approximately 3 billion years older, our research indicates that more massive galaxies build up their stars at a faster rate compared to less massive galaxies.  This discovery implies that the rate at which stars are formed is tied to the gravitational potential of a galaxy's halo, with outside evidence suggesting that this phenomenon is valid across multiple redshifts.  A computational model incorporating supermassive black holes explains these findings, supporting the idea that the growth of a galaxy's stellar mass is linked to the mass of its halo, with the black hole influencing surrounding gas to increase the efficiency of star formation.  This model predicts a 2:1 ratio of stellar to halo mass for galaxies like the Milky Way, with their mass at around 10 billion times that of our sun.  Further research is required to verify these results and expand our understanding of galaxy evolution. Introducing hybrid encoding in wireless networks, we investigated its effectiveness in resolving the difficulty of channel estimation associated with high millimeter-wave frequencies. To tackle this challenge, we developed a novel approach, called multi-group hybrid encoding (MHE). This technique organizes users into distinct groups and implements separate encoding methods for each. We propose an optimization framework to maximize the overall data transfer rate among these groups, given limited resources and hybrid encoding constraints. Notably, we observed that individual group encoding rates follow a polynomial equation, facilitating a straightforward solution. Our numerical results demonstrate that MHE significantly boosts the sum data transfer rate by an average of 88% compared to conventional hybrid encoding (HAE) when dealing with two groups, and even surpasses traditional techniques called remote estimation and near far correlation (RENFC) and remote estimation and near far correlation with partial transfer of remote data (RENT) by 109% and 52%, respectively, in various scenarios. Moreover, MHE efficiently balances the trade-off between remote data transfer power and group encoding rate. MHE's performance surpasses RENFC and RENT by 57% and 24%, respectively, in a specific case where the remote data transfer power is set to 10 dB. Our research shows that HAE is only superior to MHE when there is an extremely high ratio of remote data transfer power to noise power. We expect this finding to hold true in 6G networks, where mmWave frequencies will still pose challenges for wireless communication. A significant characteristic of Named Data Networking (NDN) is its ability to support self-management of quality of service (QoS), which has significant implications when combined with virtual machines that can operate at a higher level of abstraction. This is particularly desirable in cloud-based computing services where resources are dynamically allocated and deallocated. Our research focuses on developing efficient strategies for dynamic coordination of NDN-based cloud services, capped at a limited number of resources. Using a quasi-birth-death process, we mathematically derived the formulas for average response time, delay, and system performance as a function of available resources and showed how these can be optimized through various decision rules, including the Lagrange Multiplier and Gen Colony Optimization methods. Our results indicate that these decision rules offer improved performance over approaches that ignore resource constraints, including strategies that rely on central management and First-Come-First-Served. The findings of our study could influence the design of future NDN-based cloud services. We analyze the exponential stability of the Euler-Bernoulli beam equation on a star-shaped graph. The outer points represent the support of the beam, while the central point signifies the clamping point. A linearized version of this equation is used, resulting in an operator on a weighted Hilbert space. The stability of the system is determined by the positivity of the resolvent operator at a specific point in the complex plane. By employing graph inequalities, we establish conditions on the stability parameters and the clamping frequency that guarantee this positivity, thus confirming exponential stability. The case involving clamping at a single point reduces to a second-order equation on a linear string, while the case involving multiple clamping points reduces to a first-order equation on a nonlinear string. The stability conditions we derived align with those obtained through other methods in these specialized cases. However, our approach allows us to maintain translation invariant formulations, even in the general case. Moreover, we demonstrate that the stability exponent can be minimized through suitable choice of clamping frequencies. Finally, we provide a numerical example illustrating the calculation of the resolvent operator and confirming our stability results. Automating the selection of simulation parameters to achieve specific scientific goals is a critical challenge in modeling and simulation. The concept of utility functions originally emerged to address this issue, allowing researchers to define their objectives, and use these to guide simulations and maximize desired outcomes. This research announces an alternative dataset obtained from public Jira repositories that can be utilized for analyzing problem management processes.  This dataset offers an extensive collection of 3,822 problems based on 14,887 comments spanning across 12,114 iterations over the course of 700 projects across 280 software projects. Our recently developed method for modeling polymer structures uses a comprehensive approach based on whole programming and linear regression models. A key step in this process involves the deduction of polymer models through a series of chemical reactions that incorporate various monomers. Monomers are complex entities represented as whole programs, and our method uniquely identifies them using a proprietary algorithm, after which they are validated through a backward analysis based on the properties of desired polymers. Our approach can efficiently handle a large number of undetermined variables and monomers, and it offers precise control over predicted polymer properties, as evidenced by our simulation results for over a thousand monomers. Additionally, this program has been successfully applied to the prediction of properties in biopolymers and carbon nanotubes. More information about this method, as well as access to associated code and datasets, can be found at [www.pmx.io/deduction](http://www.pmx.io/deduction). A comprehensive user guide is currently in development. Furthermore, we outline possible future applications of our methodology, focusing on its integration with existing design software tools. Our final observation highlights the potential for our program to drive breakthroughs in multiple fields, including biotechnology, medicine, energy, and aerospace, by enabling the rapid and precise design of polymers with tailored properties. In particular, we suggest that our methodology could be utilized to create biosensors, medicine delivery systems, aerospace materials, solar cells, and other products, in addition to advancing our understanding of complex chemical reactions and free-energy models. A detailed analysis of these opportunities is planned for a future publication. As part of our current research, we are investigating the universal applicability of our whole programming method, and we are working to identify its fundamental limitations. Our future work will focus on developing whole programming methods for other important physical systems, such as metals, semiconductors, and superconductors, as well as developing program inversion algorithms that can reverse-engineer whole programs directly from experimental data. In addition, we are working on extending the program deducer to cover other types of program objects, such as programs representing particles, fields, and operators. Lastly, we outline how our whole programming method will facilitate a major paradigm shift in the field of computational science, enabling us to tackle inherently undecidable problems that currently restrict modeling and simulation techniques. Our future research will focus on resolving these decidability limitations, enabled by our whole programming method, to open up new avenues of simulation and modeling. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by achieving significant improvements in speech recognition performance, specifically a 25.5% gain, in a pandemic-related scenario where subjects learned to dual-patient breathe. We study the resonance assignments of the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons near their ground state masses, focusing on dijet production at the Large Hadron Collider. Our analysis shows that the final states of three jets and one light hadron cannot be accounted for by the $\eta$ or $\eta'$ alone, as they do not have enough energy to produce such states. However, when we consider the mixture of $\eta$ and $\eta'$, we find a viable solution that fits the available data. This etasolution provides a tangible explanation for the observed phenomena and serves as a crucial benchmark to guide future research. On the other hand, purely $\eta'$ production fails to match the experimental observations. Nevertheless, as the center-of-mass energy increases to 5 TeV and above, the contribution from $\eta'$ becomes more prominent, potentially surpassing that of $\eta$. Our study also estimates the rate at which the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons are produced in association with light hadrons, and this could be tested at the Future Large Hadron Collider. Finally, we examine the prospects for identifying the $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mesons in dark photons at the Large Hadron Collider, and our analysis suggests that the combination of $\eta$ and $\eta'$ mixing is essential to detect such signatures. On the other hand, we cannot rule out the standard model predictions for $\eta'$ production as a dark photon. Multilingual individuals have an innate ability to switch between languages, 
which is also reflected in code-mixing, the practice of combining two distinct languages.
This phenomenon is prevalent across various domains and has significant implications 
for understanding how languages interact and shaping the development of multilingual 
children's language skills; it is therefore an important area of research in 
multilingualism. Although code-mixing is common, it poses a substantial obstacle 
to language processing models, particularly in tasks like sentiment analysis and 
dependency parsing. This paper aims to mitigate this challenge by introducing an 
innovative method that leverages deep multi-lingual language models and
contextualized word representations. This approach was successfully demonstrated 
on two diverse datasets, resulting in outstanding performance and a thorough
analysis of its efficacy that identifies key factors contributing to its success. 
Notably, our method's success stems from the capacity of contextualized word
representations to capture code-mixing, as well as the ability of deep models
to process mixed sentences, despite being initially trained on separate languages. 
This breakthrough has important practical implications, opening up new possibilities 
for natural language processing in diverse, multilingual communities. We expect
this research to have a positive impact on initiatives involving code-mixed text 
and enabling various NLP tasks within these communities. Finally, we anticipate
this study to contribute meaningfully to future research in this field. 

Keywords: Multilingual, Code-Mixing, Natural Language Processing, Deep Language Models, Contextualized Word Representations.

We propose a new and comprehensive framework, complete least squares (CLS), for accurately calculating the pose of a camera in 3D from spherical image projections. Our method provides a reliable stand-alone solution for 3D pose estimation, which can be solved efficiently through a sparse optimization system. We observe that existing solutions often introduce unnecessary constraints, distortions, and inconsistencies, which hinder their performance. In contrast, our CLS approach addresses these issues, making it an ideal solution for calculating camera poses in applications like object tracking, 3D object detection, and self-localization. Our method achieves superior performance by achieving an average error rate of 0.22 degrees for pose estimation, outperforming other techniques by a significant margin of 20-60% or more, as demonstrated through the evaluation of diverse datasets including KITTI, CarPKD, and our proprietary campus dataset. Furthermore, our CLS approach significantly reduces the time required for iterative optimization algorithms, such as Levenberg-Marquardt, by up to four times, thereby facilitating faster convergence. In addition to pose estimation, our work also generalizes CLS for other computer vision tasks such as spherical calibration, 3D localization, and pose tracking, making it a versatile technique. Our research also showcases the inefficiencies of commonly used coordinate systems, such as rectangular coordinates, and proposes an innovative method for utilizing spherical projections with radian values. Our study is accompanied by an open-source C++/CUDA implementation, which is based on PPO PBF network, and can be accessed through the GitHub repository provided. Additionally, we have introduced a new campus dataset with diverse lighting conditions, including fog, sunsets, and daytime scenarios, along with corresponding ground-truth data, to ensure rigorous testing of camera pose estimation algorithms. Our campus dataset significantly surpasses the difficulty level of the CarPKD dataset, with a notable difference of nearly four times, making it an excellent resource for evaluating the performance of pose estimation algorithms. In terms of code implementation, we have proposed an innovative approach for efficiently evaluating the rotation angle of an object, which is faster and more reliable than existing methods. Our study also demonstrates the adaptability of our CLS method by showcasing its performance on various networks, including ResNet34, ResNet50, MetaNet, and PBF network, thereby highlighting its versatility. In terms of dataset analysis, we have created an open-source tool for evaluating the performance of camera pose estimation algorithms, which is based on our comprehensive evaluation criteria, and is available through the GitHub repository

To give us confidence that the estimated solution will be close enough, we established a threshold $\sigma^2 = \frac{2m\delta}{n(1-\delta)} \min\{1, \frac{(1-\delta)^2}{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}}\}$ and checked the following: if $\sigma^2$ is less than or equal to $\frac{k^2}{n}\min\{1, \frac{(1-\delta)^2}{\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{n}}\}$, then the estimated solution will be close enough, given that $m \geq k^2 n(1-\delta)^2 e^{-2}$. One significant challenge in inverse reinforcement learning lies in distinguishing between policies that are optimally optimized and those that are not, particularly when only a portion of the environment's dynamics is known. This difficulty is compounded by the fact that most existing methods are designed for settings with fully stipulated rewards or nearly optimal agents, leaving a significant knowledge gap in the field. To address this, we developed a novel Bayesian framework that quantifies uncertainty in estimating an agent's policy using only a portion of the underlying MDP's rewards. Once trained on a set of diverse trajectories from a unknown environment, our model can generate a distribution over possible policies, allowing it to accurately estimate its posterior uncertainty in the learned policy. This represents a significant advancement in the field, as previous methods typically relied on inaccurate uncertainty estimates, leading to reduced performance in subsequent downstream tasks. To test our framework, we created a series of simulated testing environments, including a simplified air traffic control domain with just three rules, and found that it consistently outperformed comparison methods across various challenging scenarios, including identifying an underlying MDP with hidden states and a mixing environment with multiple distinct reward functions. Crucially, our results indicated that the proposed framework was capable of accurately gauging the learned policy's uncertainty, leading to improved performance in downstream tasks that took this uncertainty into account. Based on these findings, integrating the proposed hierarchical Bayesian framework into existing RL methods holds significant potential for improving performance in a wide range of partially regulated environments. This could have valuable applications in real-world domains, such as designing robotic systems and air traffic management, where agents operate in dynamic environments with only partial assurance of correct behavior. By developing a systematic approach for quantifying and accounting for uncertainty in these settings, we may achieve a major breakthrough in the field. This research may also contribute to a better understanding of how to design and learn predictive models of other intelligent agents' behavior in a wide array of real-world domains. This includes scenarios such as modeling a teacher's feedback in the context of educational learning games or tracking the behavior of human participants in a driving simulation. By developing a comprehensive hierarchical Bayesian framework for capturing the uncertainty in modeling these types of intelligent agents, we may ultimately achieve a more generalizable and flexible approach to predictive modeling. This, in turn, may enable novel applications across a broad range of domains in fields like social sciences, psychology, and understanding human behavior. Additionally, this research may also pave the way for further exploration into the broader class of inverse reinforcement learning problems that involve partially regulated environments. This includes scenarios such as learning a collaborative robot

The overwhelming success of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) technologies, which offer a range of simulation-based automated control solutions, has led many to believe that DRL can replace traditional automation methods. Despite its potential, DRL's efficiency and adaptability are often hindered by several challenges including exploration-exploitation balancing, control complexity, and online learning complexity. This research aims to mitigate these difficulties by proposing a pioneering two-tiered DRL approach that tackles a control problem through a multi-step process. The first level involves employing DRL to generate a set of predefined control moves, while the second level uses these moves in a control scheme. Through this approach, we effectively address the mentioned control issues and achieve improved DRL performance. The proposed framework's effectiveness and performance are validated by practical experiments involving industrial robots, with a notable demonstration of successfully navigating a robotic arm to grasp a moving target in a complex environment. The achieved results reveal a significant advancement in DRL-based robotic control, with improvements ranging from 125% to 350% compared to standard DRL methods. The proposed solution has the potential to inspire further research in DRL, particularly in areas like robot navigation and autonomous driving. The technique is further supported by an open-source implementation of the robotic control system, which demonstrates the feasibility of the approach using real-world industrial robots, such as the AUBO Arms shown in the attached video. Over the past thirty years, preprint databases have undergone significant evolution since their inception in 1989, when the initial preprint systems were launched by LANL, arXiv, and later expanded by metadata-based searching platforms. Initially perceived as a means to accelerate publications and enable easier searching, preprints have become an integral component of the scientific workflow. Data shows that: (1) the growth rate of preprints has increased dramatically since the launch of DOIs in the early 2000s; (2) the majority of preprints are now submitted directly to the preprint server rather than being submitted to journals with a preprint version; (3) authors are typically making their preprints publicly available earlier, often within a few months of completion; (4) the shift towards earlier and broader preprint dissemination has been driven by growing internet access, decreased technical barriers, and increasing recognition from scientific communities and funding agencies; (5) while preprints have become an essential part of the scientific workflow, with over 50% of researchers actively engaging with preprints, the benefits of preprints are still nuanced and influenced by factors like scientific fields, preprint usage, and the ongoing discussions surrounding open access. We offer a systematic analysis of the development of preprint databases over the past thirty years, providing insights into the rapid growth and integration of preprints into the existing scientific infrastructure. This comprehensive context sheds light on the ongoing debates surrounding preprints. Firstly, the rapid expansion of preprints has significantly modified the conventional publication sequence, with most authors now submitting preprints to journals. Secondly, preprints have become an essential means of disseminating research findings, with increasing recognition from the scientific community and a significant portion of researchers actively engaging with preprints. Thirdly, the benefits of preprints vary depending on specific scientific fields, whereas metadata-based searching and end-to-end preprint services have uniformly facilitated preprint usage. Lastly, while preprints have become a crucial component of the scientific workflow, the final stage of publication still relies on the complex interplay between authors, journals, and publishers. This complex structure necessitates a deeper understanding of the structural characteristics of preprint databases, including preprint content, preprint links, and preprint-driven metadata, in order to unlock the full potential of preprints in accelerating the publication of scientific findings. Ultimately, the destiny of science is tied to the continued and targeted advancement of preprint databases, where the integration of open access preprints coexists with differentiated fields, preprint usage, and publication practices. High-entropy alloys, prized for their remarkable strength and flexibility, are becoming increasingly popular in industrial and scientific circles. These materials are created by combining multiple base elements in varying degrees, which often results in a multitude of possible crystal structures and properties. Our understanding and control over these properties, particularly in high-entropy alloys, are hampered by the complex interactions between their constituent elements and the difficulty in gathering precise, atomic data. This limitation stems from high-entropy alloys' unique characteristics, as well as from limitations inherent in physical and experimental methods, which can only sporadically sample the vast 'phase space' of these materials. Computer simulations, with their ability to rapidly explore vast regions of phase space, have become indispensable tools in understanding and tuning the properties of high-entropy alloys. This article surveys the progression of computational research on high-entropy alloys, highlighting advancements, existing challenges, and unexplored opportunities. We examine how machine learning algorithms, in particular, have contributed to computations, where they have proven capable of learning and predicting various properties, such as strength, from simplified data representations, often without needing detailed atomic information. While this surrogate data can be derived through computer simulations, it raises important questions about the potential for AI-driven design of high-entropy alloys, where the surrogate data may need to be supplemented with results from actual experiments or more detailed data obtained from precise microstructural analyses. Ultimately, we believe that the fusion of computational and experimental methods, facilitated by machine learning, will be crucial in unlocking the full potential of high-entropy alloys. We propose a comprehensive PDF adjustment framework that incorporates diverse data sets, including lattice QCD results, experimentally-derived values for certain quantities, and the constraints of certain processes. This framework is designed to be flexible and adaptable, allowing the use of various PDF sets, process ensembles, and regularization methods to produce a range of outputs. The framework can produce adjusted PDF sets that better satisfy certain criteria, and we demonstrate its effectiveness by employing it to incorporate the findings of the FONZ collaboration. Furthermore, we used this framework to update the NLO PDFs of Fox-Wolfram moments for parton distribution functions, and we show that incorporating lattice QCD data significantly improves the accuracy of the results. Additionally, we used this framework to examine the effect of various processes on PDF adjustment, and we found that different processes have a significant impact on the results; however, the effect varies significantly between different PDF sets. Finally, we used this framework to update the NLO PDFs of parton distribution functions while accounting for nonperturbative effects, and we show that incorporating the latter significantly improves the accuracy of the results. According to our results, nonperturbative effects are negligible at x < 0.6, but become increasingly significant at higher values of x. The framework, along with the adjusted PDFs, is available for public download at [www.helic-md.org/adjustments/](http://www.helic-md.org/adjustments/). Furthermore, the code used to generate the results is also available for public download at [github.com/HelicMD/AdjustmentsTools](https://github.com/HelicMD/AdjustmentsTools). The Helic-MD adjustment framework has been previously described in arXiv:2101.01003 and arXiv:1807.04344. The FONZ data are presented in arXiv:1806.09705. The lattice QCD data are presented in Phys Rev D 87 (2013) 014013 and in preparation. The experimentally-derived values for certain quantities were reported by Dippel et al in Phys Rev D 87 (2013) 014013. The results of the analysis of the processes were presented in arXiv:1806.09705. Interestingly, the effect of quantization varies greatly depending on the specific placement strategy used. This research aims to clarify these disparities by analyzing the connection between quantization and the neural network's effective degree of freedom. This allows us to demonstrate that binary-weight neural networks can generalize better than their full-precision counterparts under specific conditions. Signal recovery algorithms in compressed sensing often benefit from enhancements 
like stabilization techniques - damping and fractional approaches, which use 
expectation propagation to improve performance and achieve convergence. These 
stabilization methods boost long-term efficiency and enable convergence where 
it wasn't possible before. In this study, we provide an in-depth look at various 
stabilization methods and their effects, comparing their numerical performance and 
showing that a combination of procedures can significantly improve the algorithm. 

Key to our findings is the observation that a particular stabilization method 
has an intriguing link with the statistical nature of the CS problem. By 
reinterpreting this phenomenon, we develop a straightforward and universally 
effective algorithm that surpasses the performance of its individual components. 

A crucial aspect of our findings is the structure of the statistical cost function, 
which holds the key to identifying the minima of the CS problem. Although this 
structure is complex and hard to work with directly, our analysis reveals its 
composition and simplifies it, enabling the use of established optimization tools. 

Ultimately, our research not only offers an approach to solving the CS problem but 
also provides a general framework that can be applied to a broader range of iterative 
procedures, potentially unlocking new mathematical techniques and concepts. 

The code used in this research is publicly accessible via https://github.com/b-aml-Stable/compressed-sensing-stabilization.

The process of merging images from various telescopes or imaging techniques is a crucial step in creating Resolved Skymaps which are used to remove PSF artifacts in future galaxy surveys. However, determining the PSF of combined images is a complex task due to the differences in observing conditions, detector properties, and data processing of the individual images. In this research, a model is presented that characterizes the PSF of combined images using a nonlinear least-squares fit, which takes into account factors like positional offset, orientation, and scaling of the pixels, along with the variance of the pixels. The model can effectively utilize information from neighboring regions of the image and is applied to a simulation based on the Hyper Suprime-Cam (HSC) survey, though it is versatile and can be used with different types of data. The study investigates the optimal propagation of uncertainties from the nonlinear fit and demonstrates that the precision of the fit is largely dependent on the signal-to-noise ratio of the selected pixels. The model is successfully tested on real images from the HSC-XY survey, showing promising results that suggest it could significantly contribute to the development of galaxy surveys by quickly determining the PSF of combined images, which is a crucial factor in the process. The code used in this study is available at https://github.com/okawashio/PSF-prop. In the study of quantum phenomena, there are two distinct validation processes - one for quantum simulations and another for quantum algorithms. While regular validation processes typically require significant computational resources, the current approach for quantum algorithms only verifies that calculations were conducted, without confirming their accuracy. Our research introduces traditional validation methods for quantum algorithms to ensure their outcomes are precise, particularly in algorithms requiring a fixed amount of time to complete. We propose specific validation tools and provide an illustrative example of these concepts in action. Ultimately, this framework may pave the way for traditional outcome verification in probabilistic algorithms. We demonstrate the potential of this approach by showcasing a random number generator built using quantum mechanics that meets standard statistical criteria for randomness. The advantage of this method is that it yields the same results as its classical equivalent, both in time and outcome. We believe this research can give valuable insights into the relationship between quantum mechanics and randomness, and potentially unlock new applications of quantum mechanics in generating random numbers. Additionally, this research may pave the way for traditional verification of quantum simulations by checking the correspondence between quantum results and their classical versions. In the future, this research can be further developed by exploring other validation methods, such as proving that a certain property exists or demonstrating the difference between two quantities. We anticipate that these efforts will contribute to the widespread adoption of quantum mechanics in algorithm design. We also note that our approach may be applicable not only to probabilistic algorithms, but also to other types of quantum algorithms, such as those based on homomorphic encryption and quantum computing with noisy gates. We intend to investigate these possibilities in the future. We also observe that our paper relies heavily on technical details, and our description of quantum algorithms may not fully reflect the current advancements in the field. We intend to revisit these details and update our understanding of quantum algorithms, as well as the validation methods, in the future. We also note that our paper may be inaccessible to readers without a strong background in quantum mechanics, and we recommend consulting other resources for a more in-depth understanding of the subject. We also fail to fully utilize the unique properties of quantum mechanics, such as superposition and entanglement, in our research, and we intend to investigate these possibilities in the future. We also observe that our research relies on the assumption that quantum algorithm designers have a certain level of control over the outcomes, and we intend to explore the implications of this assumption in the future. Generative modeling of cell shapes can facilitate the creation of artificial cell images for training deep learning models to analyze cell morphology or or generate synthetic cells for testing cell migration in complex environments. Current methods for modeling cell shapes often rely on explicit representations, but we find them to be too restricted for capturing the diverse shapes of stem cells. In response, we propose a new method based on implicit neural representations that enables the representation of the cell shape as a continuous function, thus enabling generative modeling. Through our results, we demonstrate that this approach surpasses previous methods that use explicit representations in terms of accuracy and diversity, and we observe that it also enables the creation of cell shapes with complex features like curved edges and membrane folds. Furthermore, we find that our method improves the universality of generated cell shapes by allowing the extraction of a general shape function from a set of real cell images. In comparison studies with other models, we also find that our method reduces the discrepancy between generated cell shapes and real stem cells in terms of shape features. The benefits of our method are observed without any adjustments to the model parameters or training data. As a result, the proposed method has the potential to facilitate the large-scale synthesis of artificial stem cells, thus contributing to the development of new shape-based stem cell registration and tracking algorithms. The proposed method can also be applied to other biological cells by adapting the prior shape functions that are learned during training. The code for our method, including the Deep Learning training code and the Unified Cell platform, is available on GitHub at the specified URL. This research identifies and classifies 39 distinct types of block configurations that can be preserved by a flag-transitive permutation group, given the condition that the block size $r$ is a natural number greater than 1 and the block projection $\lambda$ is a positive integer. Specifically, these groups must act on a set partition with $r$ elements, defined over a finite set of integers $I$. Additionally, the study specifies parameters for a group to be a flag-preserving permutation group, and provides examples of groups admitted by each block configuration type. A database containing this information has been included in the research. It is further demonstrated that 18 of these group admissions are synonymous with a group admitting a semiffree permutation group, and new permutation group admission families are established. Lastly, a group admission counting upper limit is provided, and it is shown that a group can admit at most $r^{2}$ block configurations, along with an illustration using the Hofstadter sequence, a well-known example of block configurations. Crucially, this research is the first to classify block configurations preserved by a 2-transitive permutation group, and includes examples of groups admitted by each block configuration type. Notably, although it was not directly investigated, it is noted that the study's methods could be extended to non-primitive block configurations and those with a dihedral or quasi-dihedral group base. In contrast, the study finds that a group cannot admit a block configuration preserving a flag if its order is a prime number $p$ and the block size $r$ is a multiple of $p$. This research has significant implications as it can be interpreted as an extension of the Blyth-McKay theorem to block configurations. This theorem, initially proposed by Benthal in 1969, states that if a finite group $G$ has an irreducible character $\chi$ and a subgroup $H$, then the character $\chi$ cannot be split into two characters $\chi_1$ and $\chi_2$ of $H$, unless the group $G$ has an element $gh$ in $H$, such that its image in the group $H$ / Ker(\chi_1 \chi_2) is a cyclic group. This finding can be further generalized to other types of configurations. This research has important implications as it provides a complete classification of the group admissions for a particular category of block configurations preserved by a flag-transitive permutation group, and sheds light on the relationship between group admissions and other mathematical concepts, including character tables

A thorough evaluation of prediction algorithms for mapping brain regions that show consistent patterns of brain activity has identified a significant gap between theoretical capabilities and real-world performance. To address this, we develop a method to analyze empirical data sets on a case-by-case basis, allowing us to assess how well future data are expected to fit modeled relationships. This approach, coupled with multiple testing corrections, yields a more accurate estimate of prediction precision and identifies the most reliable connections for a given dataset. We apply this method to multisite resting-state fMRI data and demonstrate its value in evaluating predictive models, identifying reliable connections, and estimating expected prediction precision. Furthermore, we find that commonly used cross-validation techniques tend to overestimate prediction precision, resulting in overconfident predictions that can lead to subpar performance in subsequent studies. To facilitate replication, we provide detailed instructions for recreating our results and offer an open-source implementation of the proposed approach. This code includes custom MATLAB scripts, as well as a step-by-step tutorial, to ensure full reproducibility of our work. This research has broader implications, as it may contribute to our understanding of distinct and shared cognitive processes associated with activity in these brain regions. Fisher's fundamental theorem provides a link between genetics and evolutionary ecology by describing the interplay between genetic change and ecological competition. However, our understanding of this theorem is hindered by confusion surrounding the definitions of'speed' and 'direction' in evolutionary progress. We propose that Fisher's mean speed, which measures the average rate of genetic change, holds the key to clarifying this ambiguity. By constraining the mean speed with ecological principles, such as the law of constant evolutionary change, we can demonstrate the causal relationship between Fisher's mean direction and mean speed. Our approach resolves the long-standing debate over the precision of Fisher's theorem and offers a new perspective on the application of mathematical inequalities in evolutionary biology. Additionally, our analysis reveals an unexpected connection between Fisher's theorem and Gromov's mean impact in geometric functional theory. We argue that this connection, along with the technical difficulties it poses, may be the primary driving force behind the confusion surrounding Fisher's theorem. Nevertheless, our study shows that this challenge can be overcome by incorporating non-linear correlation into the analysis of mean impact, which in turn enables a precise calculation of Gromov's impact and reveals the inner logic underlying both Gromov's and Fisher's theorems. As a result, our work illuminates the causal significance of Gromov's mean impact in geometric functional theory and clarifies the relationship between Gromov's and Fisher's theorems. Furthermore, our study suggests an unexpected connection between evolutionary ecology and geometric functional theory, along with numerous ancillary correlations. These include links between a generalised law of constant evolutionary change, the log-Sobolev inequality, and the neuroimaging theory grounded on the heat equation, along with a fundamental inequality known as Brunn-Minkowski theory. Brunn-Minkowski theory, in turn, holds the key to unlocking major enigmas in evolutionary biology, such as the interplay between competitive exclusion and coexistence in ecological competition. We propose that our findings may also be applied to resolve other longstanding puzzles in both evolutionary ecology and geometric functional theory. Conversely, we suggest that the relationships between these two fields, along with their common underlying logical structures, may offer an innovative approach to tackling challenging problems in both the life sciences and mathematics. By combining these connections, we can potentially reveal a unified framework for addressing influential research hypotheses in both fields, along with an innovative research strategy that incorporates the principles of functional theory and evolutionary ecology. A promising approach to enhance human running efficiency is to adopt a propulsion-assisted running technique, like the one used in robotic actuators with integrated propulsion systems. To achieve high mobility frequencies, actuators must be able to generate force quickly. This is challenging for conventional electric actuators but can be effortlessly achieved by propulsion-based actuators. To take advantage of these performance benefits, it is essential to develop a control strategy that exploits the unique capabilities of propulsion-based actuators during movement. The production of mechanical power is not linear with hip joint angle in conventional running, a relationship that changes with frequency. In contrast, propulsion-assisted running reveals a linear relationship between mechanical power and hip joint angle across various frequencies. This study investigates the potential of propulsion-assisted running to improve force production and efficiency. It also examines the potential application of Vermeersch's Force Optimal Walking (FOW) control strategy to enhance mobility in scenarios with limited power supply. The FOW control strategy is shown to reduce the power requirements of the actuator by as much as 52% while still permitting high mobility frequencies of up to 4 Hz. The research provides ground for the development of more resilient and efficient bipedal locomotion systems using propulsion-based actuators. Federated learning has a unique advantage in maintaining data privacy by limiting the transmission of trained models and aggregated parameters to a central server. Nevertheless, when dealing with datasets that have inconsistent labels or no labels at all, the reliability of local models trained on unverified data becomes a significant concern. This issue is particularly pronounced in the field of semi-supervised learning, where the incomplete label information hinders the model's ability to make informed decisions. In an effort to address this challenge, we propose a new approach called CRFSRL, which safeguards against the reliability issues inherent in semi-supervised learning on the edge. This novel approach involves a data-dependent outlier detection method that uses a confidence-based threshold to evaluate the reliability of local models and reduce ambiguity. As a result, CRFSRL minimizes the amount of data transmitted to the central server, preventing data exposure and safeguarding user privacy while simultaneously ensuring the quality of the global model's training. Our experimental analysis of various scenarios in different domains demonstrates that CRFSRL offers a significant improvement in test accuracy, a reduction in communication cost, and enhanced user privacy protection. Notably, CRFSRL achieves a notable gain of up to 11.9% in test accuracy with a reduced communication cost of up to 13.9% compared to conventional approaches, underscoring its efficacy in balancing data privacy, network efficiency, and model performance. In a real-world assessment, we observed a CRFSRL performance boost of up to 10.9% in test accuracy using the CIFAR-10 dataset, demonstrating its substantial impact on model evaluation. Following a thorough analysis of parameter configurations, we identified the optimal settings that include a threshold value of 5.0 and an upper limit of 20 iterations for the Adam optimizer. These findings are expected to be of great use to researchers and developers in their future work on federated semi-supervised learning. In addition to these contributions, we have made our source code publicly available for evaluation purposes. However, there's no comprehensive, analytically-verifiable theory in high-dimensional systems that explains this trend. In our research, we develop a simple, computationally-efficient model that accurately models the behavior of these systems in their weakly-interacting regime and is capable of being solved analytically. The newly-proposed model incorporates the effects of Pauli blocking and random phase approximation in a simplified framework. The results from our model show excellent agreement with numerical simulations, thereby validating its usefulness. This article further explores and develops the concept of chiral aspects in 2dcft within the pAQFT framework, building upon a previously published study.  It specifically investigates how these aspects relate to a massless scalar field in globally hyperbolic 2-dimensional spacetimes.  The study identifies subalgebras that contain either chiral or anti-chiral observables, constructing these explicitly and showing they are embedded in the full theory's algebra.  It also establishes that the construction of these subalgebras is Cauchy surface-independent and yields a well-defined covariant theory on the space of null geodesics.  Finally, the study relates this theory to one based on null geodesics, within the context of generic, globally hyperbolic spacetimes.  A companion article will discuss quantum field theories based on null geodesics.

Consequently, this system enables educators and reviewers to utilize the proofs without relying on the Coq program, thereby allowing them to be printed or shared in other forms, as opposed to the more conventional hypertext or markdown formats. Furthermore, this tool enhances the readability of proofs by leveraging the expertise of human reviewers in annotating and distributing the proofs, as opposed to the more machine-readable.v file format. Ultimately, this system is anticipated to enhance the understanding and learning of mathematical concepts through the visualization of proofs. This is distinguished from the primary objective of showcasing the elegance of proofs, as the visual representation does not emphasize the minimaism and focussed reasoning that is typically associated with presenting proofs in the Coq program. Rather, we aim to present the proofs in a clear and understandable format that is not constrained by the conventions of the Coq program. An example of our tool's capabilities can be accessed at https://psv.informatika.ntua.gr/coq-psv/index.html. In this demo, users can select a Coq project and choose a theorem from the project to visualize its proof in an interactive tabular form. For further details on utilizing the tool, users can refer to the user guide available at https://psv.informatika.ntua.gr/coq-psv/docs/UserGuide.pdf. This system is based on the idea first introduced in Brucker et al. 2019, as described in Section 1. Notably, the proof visualization is achieved through a hierarchical structure of proof steps, as explained in Section 2. Furthermore, the tool leverages existing evidence and metadata in the.v file and the associated.i file to provide a comprehensive understanding of each proof, as discussed in Section 3. This is distinct from the minimalism of presenting proofs in the Coq program, as the visual representation emphasizes clarity and understanding over the elegance of machine-readable proofs. Specifically, the tool incorporates annotations, reviewers' feedback, and other relevant metadata to provide an in-depth understanding of each proof, as demonstrated in Section 4. We demonstrate that the fourth moment of all analytic Hecke cusp forms up to a given altitude $Q$ exceeds the fourth power of $\frac{Q^{1/4+2\delta}}{\Gamma(1/2+2\delta)^{2}}$, where $\delta$ represents an imprecise quantity less than $1/100$. The investigation relies on Sato-Tate conjecture-type hypotheses for the periods of these forms, as well as a simplified aspect of the Shimura-Taguchi relation, to establish this result. Note that the fourth moment of these forms has been estimated previously by Matsumoto and Farfalloni, yielding an inferior bound of the order $\sqrt{Q}$, while a more recent study by Li and Hou-Xuan Yong provides an enhanced estimate of $\sqrt{Q}\exp(-Q^{1/7})$. In contrast, the present investigation yields an exponential enhancement of the upper limit for large $Q$. The study assumes the Sato-Tate conjecture for Hecke cusp forms, involving a complex set of parameters, and incorporates some simplified aspects of Taguchi's work. Although a comprehensive application of Taguchi's principles would likely yield an exponential upper limit for the fourth moment, the simplified aspect of his theory employed here yields a sub-exponential upper limit. Consequently, the sub-exponential upper limit obtained here is anticipated to be near the optimal value, and we hypothesize that a similar result could hold for other types of automorphic forms. The study also relies on Matsumoto's theory of hypergeometric functions, as well as on some generalizations of the Riemann Hypothesis, to obtain its conclusions. We note that the conclusion obtained here may also have applications in the theory of integration, as well as in other branches of mathematics. Finally, we observe that the conclusion obtained here may be extended to other types of cusp forms, and we plan to explore this generalization in a future study. The present investigation can be viewed as a simplified exploration of some ideas first introduced by Taguchi, and we hope that our examination of these ideas will shed some light on the challenging conjectures involving Hecke cusp forms that were addressed by Taguchi in his work. These algorithms converge rapidly at first but may require additional iterations at interior points due to their inherent termination criteria not aligning with the primal-dual barrier's termination conditions. We introduce an alternative termination criterion, specifically checking if a directional equivalent norm becomes negligible, which indicates near-convergence in IPMs. This approach ensures that interior point iterations reach a converged state more quickly, and reduces the overall number of iterations. We demonstrate this strategy for the Conjugate Gradient method in Linear Programming, and its extension to the Preconditioned Conjugate Indoor Method for Optimal Control problems. Numerical results validate the proposed strategy leading to a significant decrease in iteration count of up to 30-40%, and occasionally no additional iterations at all. Furthermore, this improvement maintains or enhances the overall solution quality. We make the code available for reproduction of the results at a designated link. The proposed modification has the potential to decrease the computational time of IPM-based solvers. While it was implemented in the IPOPT software, this modification can be applied to other solvers with Conjugate Gradient or its variants. IPOPT users can take advantage of this modification by compiling the code with the option --no-convergence-check. Alternatively, a standalone C-function is provided at the specified link for reproduction of the results. It is possible to adapt this modification to PICO and QPSOL as well as other inner solvers with similar properties. In such cases, further code modifications would be necessary. The adoption of automated systems powered by machine learning has led to significant reliance on their functionality, with crucial processes now heavily influenced by their performance. This has created an environment where system failures can result in substantial harm, both financially and to public safety. In consequence, these errors have given rise to various forms of liability, with companies seeking to mitigate financial losses by demonstrating due care and compliance with established standards. Given the vast and rapidly evolving nature of AI technology, coupled with the technical nature of many incidents, understanding previous incidents has become essential for companies to guard against future legal liabilities. We propose the AI Incident Repository (AIRE), a comprehensive database that tracks AI system failures, aiming to prevent similar incidents by learning from existing problems. AIRE aims to provide valuable insights to both businesses and researchers, helping to avoid recurring errors and improve the development of more reliable AI systems. This paper introduces the concept behind AIRE and shares its execution, taking the form of a publicly accessible website and database of 107 incident reports, spanning 11 categories across 5 sectors. We also outline possible future developments, focusing on integrating AIRE into the digital forensic analysis of failures and utilizing its knowledge to avoid similar incidents. These developments could significantly enhance the reliability of AI-powered systems, contributing to their wider adoption while ensuring that lessons learned from past mistakes are not forgotten. We hope AIRE becomes a valuable resource for both the AI community and businesses, aiding in the avoidance of recurring errors and promoting the development of more reliable AI systems. The renormalization group plays a crucial role in understanding the nature of complex systems. Nonetheless, implementing it in practice is challenging due to the intricate procedures involved. A new precision-preserving method is proposed to run the renormalization group in practice. This method is inspired by gradient descent, a widely used technique in machine learning. By treating the removal of degrees of freedom as an optimization problem, the technique is demonstrated to be effective in studying the dynamics of statistical systems without introducing approximations. This method is then used to explore the renormalization group flow of a classical scalar field theory and a quantum electromagnetic field in four-dimensional space. The results show that the group can be accurately tracked down to very low scales, where the continuum limit is clearly visible. This is exemplified by the recovery of the classical scalar field theory's fixed point behavior. Additionally, the study reveals that the quantum electromagnetic field exhibits an unusual fixed point characteristic, distinct from both the ultraviolet and infrared limits. The recovery of the classical scalar field theory's fixed point behavior and the discovery of the quantum electromagnetic field's unique fixed point serve as demonstration of the power of this new, precise renormalization group technique. The code used to track the renormalization group is publicly available at github.com/itnovikov/rg-group-theory. To address this, our approach specifies and monitors process criteria using two distinct perspectives: operational and informational. The operational view considers actions and data, treated as integers, and the informational view looks at actions and data in terms of their meaning. The dual process monitoring method is formulated using two sets of flow conditions and an relationship that defines how these conditions interact. The flow conditions are treated as finite-state automata that generate a flow relationship graph with distinct initial and final states. The monitoring method is feasible if there's a feasible relationship state that can be reached from any initial state. If this condition is met, our approach allows processes to be monitored during execution and exceptions to be detected in real-time. The monitored process can also be modified automatically to fix problems encountered. The effectiveness of our approach is demonstrated through an example use-case based on dispute management in a business setting. Assembling de novo long-read genomic data has become more feasible due to the advancement in genomic sequencing technologies. A key challenge in this process is constructing contigs from the data in an efficient manner. Creating contigs involves resolving linearly overlapping reads, which typically requires in-memory placement of the reads to work on graph topology. This poses a significant challenge for computing resources, particularly memory, in handling sprawling graphs. To address this issue, we developed PARC, a parallel algorithm that employs a novel approach to simultaneously placing reads in memory without the need for synchronization. This allows PARC to efficiently handle a wide range of input sizes, making it suitable for assembling large-scale genomic datasets using just a few computational nodes. In our experiments, PARC demonstrated notable speedups and outperformed existing methods, achieving up to 54% faster performance, or 54% less time, when assembling human-sized genomes on 256 computational nodes. Furthermore, we demonstrated the effectiveness of our approach by successfully assembling the S. cerevisiae genome from single-mile-long long reads using 16 computational nodes, a feat previously considered impractical. This achievement not only showcases the potential of parallel computing in genomic assembly but also presents a significant hurdle for further advancements, limiting the size of the datasets that can be handled, to around 2.5 gigabases. This finding has significant implications for applying assembly methods to highly repetitive and near-repetitive genomic datasets. In order to expand the size limits, we propose the incorporation of external memory into the assembly process, a concept we plan to explore in our future research. This proposed idea is backed by notable publications in the field, suggesting that incorporating external memory into the assembly process could significantly increase the size limits by as much as three orders of magnitude. This could vastly improve our approach by allowing us to efficiently handle genomic datasets over 250 gigabases. In our future work, we plan to pursue this idea by developing an external memory-based parallel assembly algorithm that efficiently splits the dataset across memory and simultaneously places reads in memory without the need for synchronization. This will likely involve the design of novel data structures, such as linked lists, that can effectively manage memory consumption and simultaneously place reads in memory without the need for synchronization. This will likely require a significant effort and an organized approach, as evidenced by the extensive research needed to develop the widely-used Genomeseek assembly tool. By following a similar research strategy, we expect to successfully develop an external memory-based parallel assembly algorithm that efficiently handles very large genomic datasets. The LSP complements the Conditional Distribution Depth (CDD) and shares similarities with the BicDD. However, the LSP has distinct advantages over CDD and BicDD in several ways. Firstly, it enables the efficient computation of depth profiles for high-dimensional points without requiring simulations. Secondly, it results in a more stable and robust point process depth with better asymptotic properties. Thirdly, it facilitates smooth and continuous transformation of the depth function and its derivatives. Subsequently, we demonstrate the ILC transformation's efficacy in a variety of applications including effective depth ranking, regression effective depth, and an alternative to the classical Studentized range test. Our method also surpasses existing approaches in several of these applications. Furthermore, a significant advantage of our technique is its capacity to provide a closed-form estimate of the depth of a high-dimensional mean vector in a multivariate t-distribution. Additionally, we extend the concepts of depth and regression depth to cover sample sets, and showcase its usefulness in ranking regression samples. These current thresholds indicate the switching points between two distinct regimes: one controlled by aluminum and the other by niobium superconductivity. This hybrid system offers potential advantages in quantum computing, particularly in generating entangled qubits using the Asymptotic Quantum Tool Leveraging Nonabelian Operations principle. A detailed theoretical description of our findings is also outlined.

Isotopes that exhibit isochronous properties in time-of-flight mass spectrometry appear at the same instant as the reference isotopes, facilitating precise mass determination evaluations. A novel technique combines this property with the $B\rho$-defined principle, allowing for the accurate calculation of isotopic mass ratios. Our research demonstrates the effectiveness of this approach using the Lanzhou Isotope Separator Facility's beam isochronous mass spectrometer, leading to the first-ever mass measurements of the nuclei $^{54}$Ca, $^{55}$Ca, and $^{56}$Ca with significantly enhanced precision. The measured mass differences between isotopes in the same element reveal the existence of isotopic abundance anomalies, while the calculated $m_A$-corrected mass differences between elements in the same series indicate the presence of elemental abundance anomalies. These anomalies were discovered in the calcium series and correlate with the energy of the weakest resonance that enables isochronous production, suggesting that isotopic or elemental anomalies may be influenced by the resonance excitation process. Our research also includes a discussion of potential factors contributing to these anomalies, such as non-resonant excitation or the diffusion of target constituents, and the potential for the technique to reveal new information about nuclear properties and target composition using transient nuclei as probes. Finally, the accuracy of isotopic mass ratios in our study surpasses all existing evaluations, and the technique offers a promising future application for high-precision mass measurements in the field of nuclear physics. This research paper delves into the task of detecting regular expressions with predefined patterns in order to annotate and translate structured text, such as dates, phone numbers and URLs. Given the rapid evolution of regular expressions and the scarcity of labeled data, directly utilizing structured text patterns is an efficient approach to addressing this data limitation. This approach, however, poses a computation challenge as evaluating all possible regular expression patterns against structured text is inherently time-consuming. To resolve this issue, this research introduces an innovative method called R4ME, which leverages a trained transformer encoder to rapidly filter potential regular expressions and then applies a simple measurement to determine the most suitable match. In our experiments, using the MEAT dataset as a benchmark, we demonstrate that R4ME outperforms existing methods in terms of speed and accuracy, achieving a remarkable 70% increase in speed while maintaining comparable accuracy. Furthermore, we highlight the flexibility of this method by demonstrating its application to new, unseen regular expressions with minimal fine-tuning. This enhancement further improves both speed and accuracy, solidifying R4ME as a highly efficient technique for detecting regular expressions. As an added bonus, we found that R4ME is capable of accurately detecting regular expressions that were previously undetectable using traditional methods, thus expanding its potential applications in a variety of structured text analysis tasks. This research presents an in-depth analysis of R4ME, along with an implementation guideline, an openly accessible MEAT dataset and R4ME model pre-trainings, all designed to facilitate its use and evaluation. Developing a text-to-SQL parsing system that understands the meaning of written queries is a complex challenge, primarily because it demands both correct syntax and meaningful semantic interpretation. While most existing systems focus on learning semantic parsing models alone, our approach differs by incorporating a supporting task that generates meaningful text from raw data. We achieve this through a dual-model architecture that integrates a text-generation model to produce base queries, which are then refined into accurate SQL representations via a semantic parser. Our system's ability to distinguish between semantic and syntactic errors enables us to surpass state-of-the-art models in the Spider semantic parsing benchmark, particularly in the cross-domain setting. When applied to cross-domain data, our approach outperforms other methods in translating Wikipedia tables to Spider-style data, with our results indicating that high-quality base queries are essential for generating accurate SQL representations. Moreover, our analysis suggests that incorporating the Spider dataset's tables and queries, via means including table-conditioned attention and pre-trained models, can significantly enhance cross-domain performance. Finally, our analysis also reveals that incorporating additional supporting columns into the Spider dataset also facilitates cross-domain parsing. We will make our code available for reproduction of these results.

We present an efficient method to solve the High-Dimensional Rank Lasso (HDRL) problem. HDRL is a significant issue in high-energy physics data analysis but poses a significant computational challenge despite having an established mathematical proof for consistency. Our proposed method is an adaptive-sifting variant that offers significant computational savings by limiting iterations. The method achieves consistency and asymptotic equivalence to the optimal solution, thereby allowing for reliable statistical inference. The method's performance and efficiency were validated through extensive numerical simulations using real-world data from high energy physics experiments, and the results are very encouraging. The method outperforms traditional techniques significantly, often solving problems in a matter of seconds where other methods take hours or even days. The method's performance and numerical code are openly available for anyone to use. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/zzastoupk/AdaptiveSiftingHDRL. While AI is increasingly being touted as a means to achieve environmental sustainability, its actual ecological impact is often overlooked. Most studies focus on the beneficial effects of AI, such as energy savings, but rarely consider its environmental footprint. As a result, the long-term ecological consequences of AI-powered solutions are often hidden from view. This paper aims to unmask these concealed effects by investigating the systematic connections between AI-powered systems and their environmental outcomes. A comprehensive framework for understanding the ecological implications of AI has been developed and applied to analyze two prominent AI-powered applications: the prediction of nitrogen dioxide levels in London and order management in a grocery store. By examining these cases, the hidden advantages and disadvantages of these systems become apparent, highlighting the need to consider AI's environmental profile in addition to its technical capabilities. This will enable a more informed evaluation of the true ecological impact of AI-powered solutions. Ultimately, this study's framework can be used to study the environmental performance of a wide range of AI systems globally. Given the close tie between AI performance and environmental outcomes, this study suggests reevaluating the current evaluation methods of AI-powered solutions. By integrating ecological evaluation into the existing standards, the long-term environmental performance of these systems can be ensured. Business Process Management (BPM) systems rely on process mining to evaluate and improve business processes by analyzing data from various sources, including process logs and KPIs. While current process mining techniques focus on descriptive, diagnostic, and predictive analysis, there is a lack of research on prescriptive processes that recommend specific actions in real-time. This paper aims to bridge this gap by introducing a new approach: Prescriptive Procedure Monitoring (PPM). PPM incorporates prescriptive processes that suggest actions during execution, guiding the team on how to handle occurrences of anomalies, deviations from expected outcomes, or suboptimal performances. This paper outlines a framework for implementing PPM within a process-oriented business intelligence system, capturing the methodology and key challenges. To demonstrate PPM's effectiveness, we present an in-depth case study involving a real-world event where teams navigate recurring occurrences of problematic procedures. This enables planners to anticipate future problems, informing preventive strategies, and ultimately improving the process through a team-based, participatory approach. From an technical perspective, PPM tackles the preservation of process integrity, aligning with the current BPM paradigm, and addresses the perception of providing prescriptive recommendations as a form of intervention. This positions PPM as a potential catalyst for a new generation of BPM systems that integrate process-oriented business intelligence with a prescriptive component. Experimental evaluation of our PPM approach, based on a large dataset of 578 procedures from the Cholec80 dataset, shows promising results, and future work is called upon to expand and refine this new methodology. Overall, this research introduces PPM as a novel application of process mining that recommends actions during process execution, addressing the limitations of current business process management systems that fail to provide prescriptive advice. This innovative approach has the potential to improve process quality by targeting anomalies, deviations, or suboptimal performances in real-time, and our capture of PPM into a process-oriented business intelligence system marks an important milestone in the ongoing evolution of process mining. Ultimately, PPM bridges the gap between prescriptive processes and process monitoring, integrating the recommendations into a comprehensive system that includes process logging, analysis, and performance management. This positions PPM as a crucial component for team support during process execution, guiding the team on how to handle occurrences of anomalies, deviations, or suboptimal performances. Experimental evaluation of our PPM approach, based on a large dataset of 578 procedures from the Cholec80 dataset, shows promising results, and future work is called upon to expand and refine this new methodology. Due to its increased accuracy, the generalized Boussinesq model has more complex computational demands.
