Recent studies utilizing Gaia data have led to the classification of stellar objects in the Milky Way into hierarchical categories based on spatial distribution and velocity.  This research rescinds earlier definitions of "Threads" and reintroduces the term to describe extremely tenuous groups of stars exhibiting narrow velocity distributions, with velocities less dispersed than 1 km/s^3.  These threads are found throughout the galaxy, with local densities inversely correlated to galactic radius.  A systematic Gaia data analysis yielded 117 distinct threads across 306 regions of the galaxy, with a notable absence of stellar threads within the galactic bulge and regions close to prominent star-forming regions.  A proposed classification system is presented, in which threads are categorized into two distinct groups: primary threads and sub-threads.  The findings suggest that sub-threads are merely extensions of primary threads, with the latter exhibiting more coherent velocity patterns and larger populations.  A non-parametric assessment of velocity distributions within these threads reveals very low skewness values, underscoring their distinct velocity characteristics.  A primordial approach to understanding the origin of these threads is advocated, with a possible connection to the regulation of stellar clusters' velocity dispersion as they age.  A hypothetical model is proposed, illustrating a possible temporal relationship between stellar clusters and the threads.  A corresponding code is available on GitHub for reproduction of the study's results.

For the past decade, computer vision techniques have been employed to analyze and understand fashion items, achieving success in areas such as product recommendation and sales promotion. Despite these achievements, the use of computer vision in the fashion industry has several unresolved issues, with one critical challenge being the detection and correction of visual inconsistencies. This challenge is complex because it involves identifying items that do not match the expected standards, a task made more difficult by the ambiguity associated with this problem. In this context, we introduce a cutting-edge method, called VICTOR (Visual Inconsistent Item Detection with Transformers and Fashion-oriented pre-training), an application-specific model designed for transforming raw image data into feature representations that can be compared for similarity analysis. To enhance our model's performance, we also developed a corresponding evaluation dataset, consisting of 18,000 fashion item images, annotated with relevant information. Our approach, VICTOR, outperforms traditional transformer-based models, achieving a notable 4-5% improvement in accuracy, as demonstrated in our test of 8,000 unseen image items. Ultimately, the use of VICTOR is poised to revolutionize the fashion industry, enabling the effective utilization of computer vision techniques for detecting visual inconsistencies, a capability that will ultimately lead to improved fashion item quality. The proposed method will soon be made available through an open-source platform. At the time of this proposal, we have completed the following tasks: (1) designed and developed a computer vision-based model, VICTOR, for identifying visual inconsistencies in fashion items, (2) created a corresponding evaluation dataset with 18,000 fashion item images, annotated with relevant information, and (3) conducted an initial test of our approach, demonstrating its efficacy. The remaining tasks involve: (1) refining our model, VICTOR, by iterating based on feedback from potential adopters, (2) expanding the use of VICTOR to a broader range of computer vision tasks, and (3) completing the open-source platform, where VICTOR will be publicly available. The proposed research addresses these issues by developing a cutting-edge, transformer-based model, VICTOR, for detecting visual inconsistencies in fashion items, accompanied by an evaluation dataset and promising test results. The key strengths of our research include the development of an innovative, fashion-oriented evaluation dataset and the successful application of transformer models to this critical problem. The main challenge of this research involves refining our model and dataset to meet the evolving needs of the fashion industry, an issue that will be resolved by iterating based on feedback from potential adopters

A critical challenge in distributed training arises from aggregating gradient updates from multiple nodes, particularly in scenarios where synchronization and buffering are necessary. In response, we introduce the FedBuff algorithm, which surpasses existing standards by enabling the aggregation of gradient components from multiple nodes without constraints. By allowing each node to contribute all gradient components, FedBuff reveals a previously unexplored theoretical upper limit on communication efficiency. Additionally, we enhance FedBuff by integrating it with novel techniques for improving model performance, resulting in significant improvements over current standards. The objective of our research is to investigate how effective these prompts are in extracting accurate answers from unsupervised models. We have created a set of point-choice data including prompt-design information, allowing us to determine the optimal configuration for each prompt and calculate the success rate of models in a task-independent setting. The effectiveness of modern machine learning (ML) solutions relies heavily on high-quality training data. However, understanding and addressing data quality issues is a complex task, as they often have subtle effects on ML models. Existing data quality techniques primarily focus on analyzing individual data instances or small datasets, lacking the ability to address dependencies between training data and the broader ML ecosystem. To address this gap, we introduce a novel approach called data troubleshooting, which encompasses identifying and mitigating data quality issues within the entire ML lifecycle. Our proposed method evaluates the significance of each training data instance based on the overall ML performance using the Shapley value framework, allowing for a comprehensive understanding of data quality contributions. To enable large-scale applications, we also develop an efficient approximation algorithm for the significant analysis. The proposed approach is flexible and adaptable, supporting various end-to-end ML workflows, as well as multiple model types, and can be integrated into existing ML development pipelines. Our evaluation, involving real-world image classification and medical inference tasks, demonstrates the effectiveness of our data troubleshooting strategy in identifying problematic training data instances and estimating their contribution to model performance. Furthermore, we show that our proposed method outperforms existing data quality techniques, achieving up to an 8% improvement in model evaluation metrics in challenging scenarios. The proposed technique has been openly demonstrated on GitHub and the results made available on MIDS, facilitating reproducibility. With data-driven ML models becoming increasingly essential, our data troubleshooting solution provides essential tools for ensuring high-quality training data and maintaining robust ML models in diverse application domains. This paper centres around the Steklov-Robin eigenvalue problem for the Laplacian in a particular type of annular domain. Specifically, we examine a ring $\Omega_1\subset \mathbb{R}^2$ formed by two circular areas $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ where the smaller area $\omega_1$ is much smaller than the larger area $\omega_2$. We take the boundary of $\Omega_1$ to be a circle $S^1$ and denote the first eigenvalue by $\lambda_1(\Omega_1)$. We choose $\omega_1$ and $\omega_2$ such that $\lambda_1(\Omega_1)$ approaches the first Steklov eigenvalue of the unit ball $B^2(0,1)$ as the width of the annulus increases. We use the Brascamp-Lieb inequality in conjunction with a scale-invariant Soboley space to achieve this result. In addition to this, we use the same techniques and methods to demonstrate a similar result involving the second eigenvalue. However, we encounter an issue regarding the choice of Soboley norm and as such, we only manage to obtain a limiting value that is greater than or equal to the second Steklov eigenvalue of the unit ball $B^2(0,1)$. We resolve this issue and achieve the exact value by modifying the Brascamp-Lieb inequality in a way that respects a chosen Soboley norm. Ultimately, our findings provide further insight into the influence of Steklov-Robin boundary conditions on eigenvalue asymptotics. We also note that our techniques can be extended and adapted to centre around other types of eigenvalue problems in diverse geometric settings. The main challenge to the problem lies in understanding the Brascamp-Lieb inequality in the context of annular domains. Once this challenge is overcome, we believe that our findings can be expanded to various other contexts. We speculate that our methods can be utilized to centre around the complex $\lambda_1(\Omega_1)$ spectrum in the absence of symmetry, as well as to gain insights into the influence of Steklov-Robin boundary conditions on eigenvalue asymptotics in circular domains. Furthermore, we believe that our techniques can be employed to centre around the second Steklov eigenvalue $\lambda_2(\Omega_1)$. We propose an inequality for the second Steklov eigenvalue $\lambda_2(\Omega_1)$.

We show that the former can never be cost consistent while the latter, due to their ability to adjust transaction fees, can be cost consistent under specific conditions. We examine compressed, uniform flows in the solar breeze with a focus on how a uniform magnetic field influences wave behavior. Using one-minute intervals of data from the Magnetospheric MultiScale mission, we've selected instances of compressive turbulence in both solar wind and magnetosonic waves with varying magnetic orientations. When the magnetic field is perpendicular to the flow direction, discharge events exhibit a distinct $v_{\perp}$ distribution, with increased high-energy tail electrons. However, this $v_{\perp}$ distribution is diminished when the magnetic field is parallel to the flow direction. The electron distribution in these scenarios displays a distinct bi-modal pattern. The findings suggest that bi-modal electrons are an indication of compressive turbulence with a uniform magnetic field and can be identified by analyzing the electron distribution in discharge events and considering the magnetic field orientation. Since the solar wind and magnetosonic waves exhibit similar characteristics, it is likely that the bi-modal electron signature can be observed in the solar wind under specific conditions. The electron distribution in these scenarios may provide a diagnostic tool for identifying compressive turbulence in space plasmas. The study is the first to document the existence of bi-modal electrons in discharge events under these specific conditions. The data offer valuable insights into the physics of compressive turbulence and its observation in space environments. When a layer of viscous substance is shed from a slope, it forms a deposit with an inverted topography, resulting in the development of a flow channel. The geometry of this deposit plays a significant role in the flow dynamics that ensue. For instance, a concave deposit shape produces a narrow, shallow channel, whereas a convex shape gives rise to a deep, wide channel. Notably, the cross-sectional area of the channel remains constant regardless of the viscous layer's depth. The flow that forms within this channel can then be likened to a spherical cap flow. By taking advantage of a particle's ability to traverse the channel while carrying information about the flow's geometry, we have devised a method to estimate the convexity parameter, which characterizes the nature of the deposit's curvature. This technique, which we refer to as tangible optics estimation, relies on observing a particle's trajectory as it moves through the channel while simultaneously collecting data on the flow's geometry. Our research indicates that the convexity parameter can be accurately estimated using this method, particularly when multiple particles are involved. By using tangible optics estimation, we are able to determine the nature of a deposit with an unknown geometry, confirming our theoretical predictions that the cross-sectional area of the flow remains constant for both convex and concave deposits. Additionally, this method has enabled us to monitor changes in the deposit's shape over time, including during events that may weaken or alter the channel's stability. Our study provides a comprehensive understanding of the use of particle trajectories in estimating the convexity parameter, paving the way for the development of new methods in tangible optics flow diagnostics. Furthermore, this research is expected to broaden the scope of flow diagnostics, enabling it to encompass disciplines beyond geophysics and rheology. The techniques developed here, coupled with their associated strengths and weaknesses, can be applied to various phenomena that involve spherical cap flows, such as (1) meteorites and stardust as they enter a fluid on Earth, (2) microbial transport through mucus coatings, and (3) chemical reactions on spherical surfaces. Ultimately, this research is anticipated to spur the development of novel methods in tangible optics that are driven by the need to diagnose and monitor complex biological and geophysical processes. In our study, we investigate the relationship between scaling and manipulability realm, revealing that co-variance due to scaling conditions in the CRB leads to inaccurate ICP results. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a novel manifolds-based ICP algorithm, parallel to the traditional ICP, to calculate robot arm joint angles, taking into consideration both scaling and manipulability realm factors during interaction with objects. We also develop a novel, specifically designed object model, to generate synthetic data for the robot arm's state estimation sensor, while its true state is determined by the manipulability realm. Through simulations using this synthetic data, it is demonstrated that the proposed manifolds-based ICP algorithm outperforms the traditional ICP, resulting in reduced additive errors in robot arm state estimation, with the error magnitude dependent on the scale factor. The findings of this study may be generalized to other robot configurations, with the applicability extended to fields such as robotics, computer vision, and astrodynamics. Experimental validation, conducted in a physical environment, has confirmed the results obtained from the synthetic data used in the simulations. The code used for this study has been made available to the public. Generating two Higgs bosons is a critical process for understanding the mechanisms of how Higgs boson pairs are produced at large hadron colliders. We have developed a novel production mechanism for this process, and have investigated the matrix element for the interaction of protons and antiprotons resulting in two Higgs bosons and bottom quarks, using specific decay modes for $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$. Our analysis involves the reconstruction of the Higgs boson pair's mass through the collective decay products of the intermediate states $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{J}\textrm{J}'$, where $\textrm{J}$ and $\textrm{J}'$ can be $\textrm{\phi}$ or $\textrm{Z}$. We have calculated the cross-section for this interaction at the parton level, and have found it to be in agreement with previous studies. We have developed methods for identifying the Higgs boson pair through the observed distributions of the charged lepton and bottom quark in the protons' direction, and have found that these can effectively separate the signal from the background interactions. We have estimated that at the 14 TeV LHC, a 50% detection efficiency can be achieved by selecting a Higgs boson pair through the $\textrm{HH} \to \textrm{b}\bar{\textrm{b}}\textrm{W}\textrm{W}^{*}$ interaction, using a 2 sbars dataset at a luminosity of $2 \times 10^{5}\textrm{cm}^{-2}\textrm{s}^{-1}$. Additionally, our study has identified potential pathways for identifying the Higgs boson pair through its mass-dependent properties, and has estimated that a 30% detection efficiency can be achieved in a 2 sbars dataset at the same luminosity. Our work has opened a new approach to studying the Higgs boson pair's properties, and has laid the foundation for further research using this interaction at the LHC

The rapid dissemination of unprotected health information through social media platforms like Twitter poses a constant threat, resulting in the spread of misinformation that can influence users' beliefs about health. This phenomenon is exacerbated by the advent of powerful AI-generated content, which amplifies the scope of false information disseminated online. As a consequence, there is an acute need for automated systems that can not only detect protected health information but also comprehend the context of online conversations, inferring the intention behind shared content. This intent may vary; it could signify a intention to disseminate misinformation with the aim of influencing others, although individuals may inadvertently stumble upon and retweet such information. Developing an accurate classifier that distinguishes between intentional and non-intentional dissemination of misinformation is crucial, as it would enable designers to create more effective deception-detection systems, ultimately improving public health decision-making. Notably, previous research efforts in this domain have primarily centered on single social media platforms, ignoring the potential value of considering interconnected online conversations. In this context, we introduce TD4VAE, an innovative framework that identifies the acceptance or refusal of COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation within Twitter conversations and distinguishes between intentional and non-intentional dissemination. TD4VAE relies on a dialogue-based acceptance-refusal model, incorporating two key components: a dialogue encoder that captures the context of online conversations, and a vaccine-awareness model that identifies shared COVID-19 vaccine-related misinformation and their implications, all integrated into a dialogue-based acceptance-refusal model. We evaluate TD4VAE on a extensive dataset comprising 7,562 online conversations, finding it to be more accurate than comparable systems that concentrate on single social media platforms, achieving a significant gain of 4.8% in F1 score. Additionally, we engage in a detailed analysis of our model's performance, inferring that considering interconnected online conversations is essential for detecting the dissemination of misinformation. As a consequence, TD4VAE contributes to the growing literature on misinformation detection, while also addressing the associated risk of accidental dissemination, thus promoting the development of more effective deception-detection systems and informing public health decision-making. Our research focuses on the coherent control of high-energy iridium-based attosecond pulse generation via propylene gas using a 13 fs KrF laser, operating at its natural 10.6 nm wavelength. By optimizing the laser intensity and phase, we achieve a substantial enhancement of relative pulse duration, from 27 fs to 170 fs, at the expense of a reduced pulse energy. Notably, our findings indicate that this increase in pulse duration corresponds to a comparable increase in the number of produced ions, suggesting a shared recollision mechanism. To mitigate these effects, our research also examines the impact of co-propagated chirp on pulse characterization, revealing the capability to mitigate spatial inhomogeneities through a process known as field-resolved coherent manipulation. Additionally, this breakthrough in pulse manipulation could enable researchers to engage with a broader range of recollision effects, including those seen in momentum-resolved photoelectron diffraction and the coherent manipulation of ionization dynamics in multoelectron systems. The established numerical approach is then used to examine how the negative capacitance and switching performance of the FeFET are affected by varying frequencies. The analysis shows that, despite the negative capacitance being confined to a specific computational domain, it still influences the device's overall behavior and switching performance. Additionally, the study investigates the impact of different domain wall switching times on the device's characteristics and finds that slower domain wall switching times have a more significant effect on the negative capacitance effect and switching performance. Finally, the investigation looks at how the negative capacitance and switching performance are affected by changes in the ferroelectric material's properties. However, due to the complex interaction between the negative capacitance effect and switching performance, directly optimizing the negative capacitance does not necessarily improve the switching performance, demonstrating the need for numerical modeling and simulation to design high-performance FeFETs with negative capacitance. Using a test case in the Central Illinois freight network, we've refined our approach and identified key features that influence the spread of disruptions. The SHINE hadron spectrometer is designed to examine energy patterns in hadron showers both at the Large Hadron Collider and in cosmic radiation, specifically hadron showers created by high-energy cosmic rays interacting with the Earth's atmosphere. This spectrometer will utilize the shower characteristics observed at flight levels to determine precision measurements of primary hadron energy, production rates, and energy distribution among secondary hadrons. With its sophisticated tracking system composed of two planes of resistive drift chambers and high-resolution silicon detectors, SHINE excels in precision, covering a tracking area of 2.6 meters squared and supporting a vertical acceptance of 5 degrees. This comprehensive system, combined with a calorimeter capable of sampling 6-7 interaction lengths, enables SHINE to examine shower development in great detail, making it an exceptional instrument for answering key questions in shower physics and high-energy cosmic ray physics. This paper discusses the design, development, and performance of the SHINE hadron spectrometer. SHINE is currently installed on the JINR's lead-tungsten calorimeter, situated at the CERN, in preparation for operations at the Large Hadron Collider and in-flight tests to commence in 2019. This paper will also discuss ongoing and planned tests. Additionally, with its adaptable design and comprehensive capabilities, SHINE can easily be adapted to in-flight operations, featuring a unique, compactized design that will enable it to detect the characteristics of hadron showers created by high-energy cosmic rays interacting with the Earth's atmosphere at flight levels. This compactized design will feature a tracking system composed of two planes of resistive drift chambers connected to a thin silicon detector, along with a sampling calorimeter, all combined within a portable, 16 cm thick cube. This compactization will enable SHINE to participate in a series of flight tests starting in 2019, where it will demonstrate its capabilities in in-flight operations and become a key component in a new generation of portable hadron spectrometers. Despite their accomplishments, they struggle with gross orientation transformations between input images and classification models. Recent studies have introduced Orientation Convolutional Networks (OC-Net) to tackle this issue by incorporating oriented filters, resulting in improved performance compared to traditional Deep Convolutional Networks (DC-Net). This study analyzes OC-Net and proposes novel variations to further enhance its capabilities. By applying the Steerable Filter Transform (SFT) to evaluate filters' circular symmetry, the research can identify and modify or replace them. Based on this discovery, the study modifies OC-Net to remove circularly symmetric filters and enhances its overall effectiveness. The proposed networks are evaluated on the CIFAR-10 and ImageNet datasets, achieving superior performance with equivalent or decreased computational resources. The associated source code can be accessed at https://github.com/JAD-ML/Orientation-DeepNet. The study also introduces a novel evaluation metric to assess OC-Net performance and provides a detailed comparison with existing methods. The findings show that the proposed networks outperform other state-of-the-art models in terms of accuracy, parameter count, and computational requirements. The study demonstrates the significance of designing oriented filters in OC-Net and presents two novel architectures, named Deep Steerable Network (DSN) and Deep Steerable Pooling Network (DSP), to complement the existing DC-Net. When evaluated on the CIFAR-10 dataset, the proposed DSN and DSP models achieved superior performance compared to DC-Net with reduced parameters and computational requirements. The study presents a thorough ablation study and offers multiple variants of the Steerable Filter Pooling (SFP) layer for image identification. The success of Deep Learning methods in computer vision and image processing has created significant expectations for their adoption in point cloud processing. Despite several attempts at developing graph convolutional networks, a reliable and general approach has yet to be established due to the complex and variable nature of point cloud data. One of the primary challenges lies in defining an effective graph topology that captures inter-point relationships, a problem exacerbated by the redundancy often present in data captured through sensors such as LiDAR or RGB-D cameras. This paper proposes a novel approach to point cloud processing that relies on a simplified yet efficient graph topology, built by merging nearby clusters of points and utilizing their local characteristics to inform global connections. Our method focuses on classifying point cloud data into superpoint clouds, with the aim of ultimately enabling scene segmentation and object detection. Experimental results on the Semantic3D dataset demonstrate our approach to be both efficient and reliable. The proposed method achieves an accuracy of 8.14% - 8.60% (depending on the dataset version used) on a point cloud classification task, surpassing multiple baseline models, including those that rely on fixed adjacency matrices and attention-based methods. The code and pre-trained models are available for download at the repository link at the end of this abstract. Our approach represents a significant contribution to the development of effective graph convolutional networks for point cloud processing. It offers a versatile and efficient solution to the challenging problem of point cloud classification, with implications for object detection and scene segmentation. The reliability of our results is further enhanced by the use of a precision-based clustering technique that minimizes overlap, allowing us to focus on distinct classes of points cloud. Second, we employed a simple yet efficient strategy for merging nearby point cloud data into superpoint clouds. Finally, we used a local characteristic-based approach to inform global connections in the graph, proven to be more effective than other attention-based methods. Trojan assaults are highly challenging to detect because they disguise their malicious code within unrelated apps, awaiting command from a commander to trigger the attack. Existing methods that attempt to mitigate this issue can be bypassed by relying on specific images, entailment relationships, or word embeddings which are all ineffective in the real-world scenario where attackers use diverse means to execute the attack. We propose a new approach to tackle this issue in image and natural language processing contexts by developing a method to identify unique semantic patterns within Trojan assaults. The nature of core formation in terrestrial planets is significantly influenced by the types and efficiency of planetary core accretion and differentiation processes. Studies of exoplanetary masses and orbital periods suggest that some planets may have sizes consistent with maintaining partially melted cores or even entirely molten interiors. This study aims to utilize the spectral analysis of host stars to assess the possible sizes of partially melted cores in terrestrial planets.

We carried out an in-depth analysis of 13 elements in a sample of 30 bright G-dwarf stars hosting terrestrial planets, yielding precise measurements for their elemental abundances, accurate to within 2%. This led to the development of two models to predict exoplanetary core sizes based on mass and orbital period.

Our findings indicate that most planets in our sample have sizes ranging from 0.5 to 1.5 Earth radii, with some extending beyond this range. Approximately half of the planets in our sample appear to have partially melted cores or entirely molten interiors, compatible with a wide range of orbital periods and masses, with some extending beyond 1.5 Earth radii.

Our predictions that small, rocky planets can maintain partially melted cores or entirely molten interiors align with other research and suggest that core-peltion models may need to be readjusted to account for various planetary configurations and processes. Deep neural networks (DNNs) have been used for wireless signal simulation, but their traditional architecture may hinder further improvement in performance, leading to increased complexity and deeper networks. This has prompted research in modified DNN architectures, such as attention mechanisms (AMs), which enable more efficient feature extraction. However, AMs are typically grid-based and cannot be applied directly to 2D channel state information (CSI). This paper introduces a novel AM for CSI, called the cross-correlation attention mechanism (Ccam), which utilizes the cross-correlation between CSI maps to generate weighted feature maps. Ccam is then combined with a U-Net based wireless position estimator to enhance its performance. Experimental results show that the U-N-Ccam model outperforms the U-Net model and a comparable grid-based AM model. Moreover, the U-N-Ccam model exhibits better scalability and a significantly lower parameter count than the grid-based model. This research is the first to apply AM to CSI, opening up opportunities for future improvements in wireless signal simulation. The main ones are the weak and strong Kleisli categories, which represent the modal logic based on weak and strong composites in topological categories. A key finding is that the same strong Kleisli category can correspond to different weak Kleisli categories, demonstrating the importance of topological categories in modal logic. The study further encompasses the advancement of categories of modal structures equipped with orders, which is foundational for developing first-order modal logic. One of the primary obstacles in AI research lies in measuring ambiguity within a system. Yet, uncertainty and error are consistently interchanged in scientific literature without thorough justification. This misuse of terminology might stem from the fact that both uncertainty and ambiguity are often employed as synonyms for vagueness, although they have distinct meanings. Uncertainty refers to incomplete knowledge, whereas ambiguity concerns the lack of clarity in expression or meaning. This work undertakes a comprehensive evaluation of existing approaches to identifying ambiguity in computational systems. It systematically assesses both classical and quantum ambiguity metrics, along with their underlying assumptions. Furthermore, the research presents an objective standard for evaluating ambiguity in algorithmic processes. Ultimately, the investigation demonstrates that the vast majority of known techniques are ineffective in detecting ambiguity, while also outlining potential future directions for development. This study will serve as a benchmark for evaluating novel methods to identify ambiguity in computational systems. In addition, the research discusses implications of ambiguity, citing well-known examples from physics and mathematics, and highlights its significance for supporting the holistic development of intelligent systems. The latter point is particularly pertinent in the context of discussions surrounding standardization in AI research. The research may therefore contribute to further discussions on the topic. The text examines two possible avenues for further exploration, each corresponding to a distinct interpretation of quantum ambiguity, namely the probabilistic and the non-probabilistic approaches. Finally, the investigation highlights the interconnection between ambiguity and negative information, while also emphasizing the distinct significance of non-ambiguous systems in both machine learning and statistical inference. Throughout the text, an attempt has been made to provide an accurate overview of the current state in the field, along with clear illustrations that demonstrate the difference between uncertainty and ambiguity, using fundamental results from quantum logic and epistemic quantum theory. The research may thus enable readers to appreciate the distinct contributions of both classical and quantum approaches to identifying ambiguity, along with their respective applications to intelligent systems. The text concludes by outlining future research directions, addressing questions such as whether standard amplification can ever lead to detection of ambiguity in systems and whether quantum ambiguity can ever be pinpointed in systems. Alongside these theoretical investigations, the research also explores connections to relevant concepts in quantum logic and epistemic quantum theory, while also examining the possibility of uncovering non-ambiguous states in systems that possess positive entropy. The text may thus provide a valuable contribution to the discussion on standards in AI research, while also deepening our understanding of the intricate link between quantum logic and epistemic quantum theory, along with the distinct interpretations of quantum ambiguity. Effective methods are required to determine the optimal simulation duration, but this poses an inverse problem due to the arbitrary nature of output values, making it difficult to define a objective function. This issue is overcome by utilizing image processing and machine learning techniques to quickly evaluate simulation progress. We propose using pixel changes in graphical outputs as a measure of advancement. This approach leverages machine learning to analyze image regions and assess similarity. As a result, the optimal simulation duration can be quickly determined within the hundreds to thousands of time steps, facilitating large-scale simulation runs. Our methodology is versatile and can be applied to various types of graphical outputs. Additionally, we cap the memory consumption at 768 MB to maintain scalability. The benefits of our approach are significant, allowing for substantial increases in the number of simulations run within a given time frame. The maximum number of simulations can be maximized by performing 512 unique Monte Carlo simulations, with each starting with a distinct set of parameter values and a corresponding time step, on a standard 64-bit system with 8 GB of RAM. A study of modifications to high-energy jets in heavy ion collisions at the Large Hadron Collider has been conducted. Analyzing collisions of protons and lead ions at 5.02 TeV, researchers discovered variations in the behavior of jets associated with a high-energy photon in both proton-proton and lead-lead collisions. When these variations are measured in events containing at least one additional charged particle, produced as a result of the collision, the data indicates significant alterations to the internal structure of high-energy jets. Unlike text, mathematical expressions have a consistent framework driven by mathematical operations and symbols. However, the act of writing them involves complex hand movements that vary significantly in speed and trajectory. This study presents an innovative approach using median analysis to develop synthetic speech lengths, excluding frequency-based acoustic models. A database of synthetic speech variations was established by modifying the speaking rates of five male and five female speakers from the CMU Arctic dataset. Subsequent examination of this data revealed that speech from various lengths could be distinctively separated based on median length. Building upon this discovery, a train-only framework was developed to create synthetic speech lengths. This method first segments speech into equal-duration units and reassembles them based on a median analysis-driven binning strategy. As a result, this framework bypasses the need for complex acoustic modeling and statistical training. Additionally, the created synthetic speech lengths are claimed to be unique and distinctively perceived by human listeners. The efficacy of this approach was verified through comprehensive listening tests and comparisons with a deep learning-based method, revealing superior preservation of the original speech samples using the median-driven approach. Moreover, the study includes quantitative evaluations of the proposed method, demonstrating an average 57% reduction in computational complexity while maintaining superior speech quality. The findings of this study could potentially lead to increased efficiency in speech processing software development. This paper presents spHabitat, an R tool designed to address this limitation and efficiently handle single-species, multi-species, and integrated model approaches for species distribution analysis. It also offers an optimization technique and simulation tools to facilitate model interpretation and selection, along with a case study demonstrating its applications. Furthermore, the package's source code and documentation are freely available at https://github.com/ghandry/spHabitat.

This highly distorted view reveals multiple features within the equatorial plane of the galaxy, showcasing a sinusoidally shaped dust lane at the center.  Additionally, a pair of symmetric, neutral outflows is observed at the edges of the galaxy, close to the dust lane's symmetry axis.  At a distance from the dust lane equivalent to 5-6 kiloparsecs, the outflows change direction, shifting towards the source of the dust lane's emission.  Based on the outflows' shape and motion, scientists propose a model in which gravitationally bound outflows propel material perpendicular to the equatorial plane, influencing the observed neutral features within the plane.  This discovery supports theories of galaxy evolution that involve star-driven outflows impacting a galaxy's interstellar medium, and the observed distortion provides new perspectives on dust extinction and emission patterns in the equatorial plane of the galaxy. Its core design focuses on fulfilling a number of requirements which facilitate high performance, flexibility, and user interaction. The McMini tool accommodates a range of features including multiple shared variable models, thread prioritization, and custom thread scheduling policies. The incorporation of these features into McMini reflects their potential implementation difficulty. The use of this methodology allows us to achieve a substantial reduction (of two to three orders of magnitude) in the size of the McMini statespace, and consequently, in the tool's running time. The global WhatsApp crisis began in 2019-2020 when several countries experienced widespread misinformation spreads within local communities via the app, particularly concerning viral myths linking COVID-19 origins to conspiracy theories. In an effort to combat this issue, WhatsApp introduced several measures to limit message sharing. The primary goal of this study is to assess the impact of these changes. By collecting and analyzing public WhatsApp chats in India, our research investigates two primary aspects: the overall effect on misinformation circulation and the diverse messages exchanged among users. Our findings indicate both a decline in forwarded messages and a decrease in the spread of conspiracy theories related to COVID-19, primarily resulting from high-ranking users promoting publicly available news content. Conversely, the majority of regular users continue to engage with misinformation, highlighting the challenges in ensuring app users become reliable news sources. Our research outcomes support the WhatsApp initiative and suggest further optimization strategies to enhance the app's misinformation mitigation capabilities. Furthermore, our analysis provides valuable insights into understanding the spread of social misinformation within private online communities. The combined approaches of social science and natural language processing used in this research yield valuable insights into examining app or platform features and their effectiveness in combating misinformation. Moreover, our investigation contributes to understanding the ongoing global WhatsApp crisis and offers concrete recommendations for feature design and optimization to combat misinformation within private online environments. Modern network defense tools rely heavily on evolving protocol formats that change rapidly to maintain effectiveness, thereby ensuring the seamless identification of these tools by other systems and security tools. Despite this necessity, some manufacturers of closed-source tools and some open-source tools like Nmap are disregarding the standards of adaptive protocol identification by sticking to outdated detection methods that become less effective over time. This disregard not only compromises security but also creates vulnerabilities, as demonstrated by recent research which discovered and exploited multiple detectable vulnerabilities in Nmap. This research successfully subdued adaptive detection in prominent network monitoring tools, highlighting the importance of updating detection methods to ensure continuous protection. This new approach could be a game-changer in the world of network security, forcing manufacturers to reconsider their strategy and bring adaptive protocol identification to the forefront. To facilitate this change, we outline our methodology for identifying vulnerabilities and introducing new, innovative features that utilize adaptive identification, thereby illustrating its extensive capabilities. This research serves as a warning to manufacturers of network defense tools that stick to traditional detection methods, urging them to shift towards adaptive identification to stay ahead in the market. A beneficial approach for gathering user contributions to a machine learning model is federated learning, as it enables global model training using locally stored data, with users contributing to the model at a central location. When employing federated learning with users having access to diverse data, novel categories may arise for the model to learn, presenting a situation referred to as zero-shot federated learning. This learning method is challenging due to the requirement that models generalized well across various data distributions, especially when encountering unfamiliar categories. In this study, a solution to the 1-shot N-way classification problem in audio domains is proposed, by combining the advantages of multi-head attention, transformer architecture, and meta-learning techniques. Experiments have been conducted using three datasets, comprising speech, music, and bird sounds, with the findings indicating that the proposed model achieved superior performance compared to baseline techniques, by accurately classifying novel categories with up to 20 novel categories and 5 novel data samples per class. The model's efficiency was further demonstrated by its performance of training within a central location, using a typical GPU, within 10 central location iterations. Furthermore, the implemented approach demonstrated robustness when employing a mixture of training data originating from the same domain but containing the novel categories (a mixture of training data), as well as when encountering unfamiliar acoustic patterns entirely (exclusively novel data). In addition, the model's generalizability was further validated by its performance using various parameter settings, with notable consistency when employing similar models but with random parameter initialization. The study's findings suggest that the proposed model offers a practical solution to the 0-shot N-way classification problem in audio domains, serving as a useful reference for federated learning applications. This study analyzes regional variations in COVID-19 coverage within the United States, exploring correlations between news stories, infection rates, fatality rates, and audience size. Using a dataset of nearly 15,000 news articles from 392 areas, covering all 50 states, we quantify COVID-related content among 173 other topics. Our research reveals that regions experiencing higher infection and death rates received more COVID-related coverage, with local news outlets providing greater coverage than national ones. Interestingly, areas with larger audiences received more COVID coverage, despite similar reporting rates from national and local outlets. These findings provide essential insights for researchers and practitioners working in computational modeling, health communication, and news production. By understanding factors that influence COVID coverage, we may better assess the impact of news on public perception and decision-making, especially regarding critical topics like the pandemic. We develop a novel theoretical framework to examine how traditional recurrent neural networks and their transformer counterparts learn to count in sequence. Our approach utilizes a random memory matrix that simulates the internal workings of these networks. Our results indicate that the diagonalization of the random memory matrix plays a crucial role in accurate counting, and that the presence of a dominant eigenvalue significantly impacts this process. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the internal state vectors following the diagonalization can be arranged in a hierarchical order, which in turn enables sequential counting without the need for explicit weight updates. Our findings are substantiated through extensive experiments involving both synthetic and real datasets, and our analysis offers insights on the characteristics of the memory matrix that facilitate successful counting. Our empirical observations suggest that networks with specific memory properties are more likely to exhibit robust counting capabilities even in the presence of adversarial attacks. Our research contributes to the understanding of the underlying mechanics of modern neural networks and may lead to the development of enhanced memory designs to boost counting performance. In recent years, various exact, filter-based data structures have been introduced to support efficient lookup operations. Among these, Bloom filters offer a balance between computational resources, memory usage, and false positive error rates. However, their property of being monotonic is inconvenient since any change to the filter necessitates a reconstruction of its bits. Conversely, Bloom filters can be adapted through the insertion of complementary elements, though this incurs increased computational and memory costs. To address these shortcomings, we present (a) Xor Filters: modified Bloom filters incorporating monotonic properties and simplified calculation schemes; and (b) updated Cuckoo filters incorporating the reconstructed Bloom filters for enhanced performance. Additionally, we examine the impact of using hash functions with properties other than independence, specifically, random Xenon hash functions. Our findings indicate that inserting complementary elements after using random Xenon hash functions reduces the need for filter reconstruction, thereby decreasing both computational and memory costs. Ultimately, we embark on an in-depth analysis of the trade-offs between computational resource, memory usage, and false positive error rates to guide practitioners in their selection. However, previous research on deep SNNs has primarily focused on adapting existing models, such as convolutional neural networks, without considering the constraints of biological neural connections. In contrast, our study takes a novel approach and develops a novel deep SNN architecture that facilitates both efficient data processing and viable pattern learning. By strictly adhering to the rules of valid spiking connections, our model allows for significant weight pruning, thereby ensuring biological plausibility. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the effectiveness of our model in learning complex patterns, such as the MNIST dataset, using the backpropagation-in-time algorithm and an advanced training method specifically designed for SNNs. When tested on a Texas Instruments processor, our findings reveal the benefits of our model in terms of both computational efficiency and energy performance. In comparison to a similar CNN model, our SNN model exhibits superior energy efficiency but slightly higher latency. In the future, we aim to expand on this research by exploring other biological constraints and adapting our model for use in inference tasks. Additionally, we intend to investigate the potential of our model for addressing challenges in pattern learning, such as data representation and classification. With further development, we are confident that our model will enable spiking neural networks to accurately replicate the learning processes observed in biological brains. In doing so, we will be one step closer to unlocking the long-standing secrets of how the human brain processes information. Value-based decision-making approaches often struggle with uncertainty, particularly when they rely on incomplete or imperfect feedback from the environment. This work addresses a critical issue in autonomous systems by developing an adaptive method to identify and isolate unexpected changes in dynamic systems that affect their reward structure. Building on prior research in partially-observed Markov decision processes (POMDs), this study introduces a novel framework that incorporates uncertainty due to incomplete observation and unexpected environmental alterations. An efficient algorithm is developed to solve this problem, using a dynamic programming approach that takes advantage of the POMD structure. A hydroxyl-linked interface displayed a significant band bend with electron accumulation and InAs gap reduction, whereas a fluoride-linkage produced electron loss and InAs gap increase. Deep, wide, and complex Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) are increasingly being employed for image classification tasks at the Click level (i.e., data granularity). However, such architectures pose significant challenges for model training, including increased computational costs, memory consumption, and data management complications. In response to these issues, researchers have proposed various model pruning techniques to accelerate inference. Nevertheless, these methods have generally focused on compressing models for inference purposes only, disregarding their usability for training. As a result, previously proposed methods either destroy the original model, limiting its deployment to inference only, or skip the evaluation of the pruned model's effectiveness in training. To address these shortcomings, we introduce ClickTrain, a cutting-edge, detailed, and precise model pruning method designed to support both inference and training operations on the pruned model without data loss or computational overhead. ClickTrain achieves this through a sophisticated, iterative process that reorders model Clicks based on their sensitivity to adaptation, striking a balance between compression ratio and model structure preservation. We then use this approach to create a sequence of detailed, progressive pruned models that facilitate training, allowing the model to adapt to the data without plateaus or training stagnation. We demonstrate the effectiveness of ClickTrain through comprehensive experiments on widely-used image classification datasets, yielding a significant improvement in the pruned model's convergence speed (up to 30% faster), along with an acceptable compression ratio (up to 27%), all while maintaining the original model's accuracy in inference. Upon establishing this, we prove that there are infinitely many primes which are the sum of two squared integers of equal parity, where the lower of the two squares is less than half the prime itself. Following this, we combine previously established results with the parity argument to show that there are infinitely many twin primes. This reasoning stems from the fact that a prime number 2n+1, which is odd, can be expressed as the sum of two squared integers of equal parity, where the lower of the two squares is n. Consequently, there are infinitely many primes that can be expressed as the sum of two squared integers of equal parity, where the lower of the two squares is less than half the prime itself. Similarly, there are infinitely many primes which are the sum of two squared integers of equal parity, where the lower of the two squares is greater than or equal to 17. This, combined with the parity argument, yields an infinite number of twin primes, where the prime 2m+1 can be expressed as the sum of two squared integers of equal parity, where the lower of the two squares is m. Ultimately, we show that there are infinitely many 7-digit, 9-digit, and 11-digit twin primes through this approach, where the prime 10000n+2 can be expressed as the sum of two squared integers of equal parity, where the lower of the two squares is 16n+1. One type of data that has recently gained significance is the existence-absence data where each sample can possess any number of categorical or binary characteristics denoted as \emph{features}. This data type is commonly encountered in molecular biology, network data, and image analysis. Unlike traditional numerical data, analyzing existence-absence data is more complicated as it involves treating each sample as a subset of a total set of possible features. This uniqueness necessitates the adoption of specialized algorithms, often based in combinatorial mathematics that treat existence-absence data as a union of total feature sets. In this research, we evaluate the efficacy of seven existing clustering methods including the use of information matrices, spectral clustering based on graphs induced by the sample's binary similarity matrices, and deep learning-based methods designed for union-like data. Our analysis involves an extensive simulation study where we create a diverse range of datasets to test the performance of each method. Our findings indicate that the applications of the standard spectral clustering algorithm and its variants are limited to data with a small number of distinct features. Conversely, the effectiveness of algorithms that explicitly consider the union-like nature of existence-absence data, such as SCADE and DeepUMAP, yield better results in our simulation study. This research is significant as it highlights the possibility of using existing clustering algorithms to analyze high-dimensional existence-absence data. Ultimately, we recommend the use of SCADE and DeepUMAP for their superior performance in our simulation study. Our source code is publicly available at https://github.com/corralab/scade. Handwritten Text Recognition (HTR) with limited resources is a challenging task, largely due to the scarcity of labeled data and limited language knowledge (dictionaries and language models). While data annotation is expensive, language knowledge can be utilized to generate synthetic data, but existing approaches often fail to accurately mimic real-world labels, leading to inadequate results. A novel approach is proposed to tackle this problem, leveraging the attributes of Plastering and Pasting to complement existing data augmentation methods, addressing the need for single-image supervision in unsupervised HTR tasks. Experimental findings on the datasets, liberty mutual dataset and historical dataset from the National Library of Australia, demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. It outperforms baseline approaches, particularly on the liberty mutual dataset, where its performance closely resembles that of a model with access to ground truth during training. Furthermore, it shows a significant improvement in characters, words and line recognition compared to the baseline model, with results similar to that of a model with access to ground truth on the national library of Australia dataset. While showing promising results on the liberty mutual dataset, its application on the national library of Australia dataset reveals room for improvement, especially when compared to a model with access to ground truth, indicating that the proposed method alone may not be enough to overcome deep-set biases in the dataset. Thus, a potential future direction is to investigate how the proposed method can be utilized in conjunction with other approaches to further enhance its performance. We examine the compactness of composition mappings between Bergman spaces associated with certain types of convex domains in complex n-dimensional space. To do this, we consider properties of the mapping's determinant and its first derivative, specifically its behavior on the boundary. By establishing these conditions, we obtain necessary and sufficient requirements for the compactness of composition mappings between these spaces. Our approach relies on a combination of two tools: a formula for determining if a function is bounded within a certain region, and a property of analytic discs that involves a projection onto a complex line. Furthermore, our method of analysis allows us to consider more general compositions involving analytic functions that may have singularities within the region's interior. A key application of our findings is the study of biholomorphic equivalence between certain types of convex domains in complex n-dimensional space. To demonstrate the practical use of our results, we show that the Poincaré disc is not biholomorphically equivalent to the upper half-plane, even though they have the same topological properties. Finally, our work is accompanied by a set of open problems and challenges for further research. With these problems, we aim to expand the scope of compactness theory in Bergman spaces and understand more complex composition mapping phenomena. Additionally, we propose investigating the same problems in the context of Hardy spaces, as well as exploring the same questions in the presence of additional singularities within the region's interior. By addressing these challenges, we can deepen our knowledge of composition mapping and its relation to determinant and derivative properties, ultimately facilitating a more comprehensive understanding of this powerful mathematical tool. Lastly, we outline a possible research strategy to tackle these issues.

Statistical inference is based on a conceptual framework that uses likelihoods to compare hypotheses based on data, however this concept has weaknesses as it is not invariant to modeling changes and does not address the issue of high dimensionality in complex data sets. A specific type of likelihood, the circular likelihood, has been proposed as an alternative by Darling and Atchadé in 2001. This type of likelihood is characterized by its lack of increase along cycles in a graph. In this study, we demonstrate that commonly used statistical models have circular likelihoods. Furthermore, we show that non-transitive circular likelihoods, which exhibit cyclic relationships, exist in these models. A particular example is the t distribution with degrees of freedom less than two, which has a non-transitive circular likelihood. In this research, we examine the effect of restricting the standard Bayesian posterior distribution to the set of admissible hypotheses based on high marginal likelihoods. A key finding of this study is the proof that this restricted distribution is proper whenever the likelihood is circular and has a non-transitive nature. Another key contribution of this research is the development of a simulation method to generate random hypotheses based on high marginal likelihoods. In this study, we apply the concept of circular and non-transitive likelihoods to two widely used Bayesian methods, the Laplace mixture model and the skew-t model. A proof is provided in the supplementary materials. This study also includes a simulation based on real data in fields such as astrophysics and music. The results show that the standard Bayesian posterior distribution performs similarly to the restricted distribution in these applications, however the latter excels in situations of high complexity. In this research, we propose two novel approaches, the direct sampling method and the indirect sampling method, to generate random hypotheses based on high marginal likelihoods. The direct sampling method uses specialized algorithms such as the Hamiltonian Monte Carlo method to sample directly from the standard Bayesian posterior distribution, while the indirect sampling method first generates random hypotheses and then assigns them a probability based on their relative likelihoods. In this study, we demonstrate that the indirect sampling method is more efficient than the direct sampling method, especially in situations of high complexity. A key contribution of this research is the proof that the standard Bayesian posterior distribution is consistent under certain conditions, particularly that the likelihood space is compact and that the prior distribution is regular. In this study, we show that the standard Bayesian posterior distribution is consistent in two commonly used statistical models, the skew-t model and the Laplace mixture model. A proof is provided in the supplementary materials.

Evaluating inter-beat intervals (IBIs) in electrocardiograms (ECGs) allows clinicians to identify cardiovascular diseases and monitor their progression. Moreover, this approach enables adaptable and efficient heart rate assessment, enabling real-time monitoring and diagnosis. The proposed methodology is made accessible through open-source code, allowing for reproducibility and further development. Our findings emphasize the significance of this deep learning technique for enhancing cardiovascular disease diagnosis and management, while minimizing costs associated with computational resources. Additionally, this work highlights the potential of 2D wavelet transform in augmenting deep learning methods, thereby validating the integration of traditional signal processing techniques with cutting-edge machine learning approaches. The active Ornstein-Uhlenbeck particle (AOUP) is a simplified model that incorporates both active movement and random motion to study collective behavior in particles that adapt to their environment. In this study, we explore the effects of varying the labor parameter, which represents the strength of the particles' response to their surroundings, on the AOUP's dynamics. Our findings reveal a profound change in the system's behavior as the labor parameter shifts from a high-value regime to a low-value regime. In the high-value regime, the particles exhibit a collective freezing transition, characterized by a sharp increase in their overall polarization when near their environment's boundary. In contrast, the low-value regime shows no evidence of a freezing transition, with the polarized state relaxing more gradually. Additionally, we observe a shift in the system's dynamics from a single, dominant timescale to a more complex structure of timescales, facilitating a deeper understanding of the underlying physics. Our research uses three distinct methods - exact solution, dynamic mean-field theory, and simulations - to study the system's behavior in different regimes. Our study provides a foundation for investigating collective particle dynamics in various active matter systems. Furthermore, our work may be applied to other systems, such as colloids and bacteria, subject to different types of active movement models. By mapping the phase diagrams of these systems, we hope to gain a more detailed understanding of their underlying physics. To facilitate cross-lingual transfer in NLP, researchers often rely on data-based approaches or property-sharing hypotheses. We introduce a model-independent framework that leverages neural networks' behavior to achieve this transfer. By training task representations on multilingual text data, we enable networks to exhibit similar task performance across languages, both in and out of their training languages. We demonstrate effective, universal generalization from English to German and other languages, including sign language, using only text data. We show that our approach can be adapted to other NLP tasks, such as sentiment analysis, and propose a method to automatically create task representations from network embeddings. We provide thorough analysis and assessments of the challenges and limitations of our framework. Ultimately, we argue that capturing task representations is essential for understanding how networks operate and can facilitate cross-lingual transfer. A common approach in video super-resolution is to utilize a encoder-decoder architecture in conjunction with a self-similarity loss function, which generates the input video's frequency spectrum and applies a matching function to calculate the lagged similarity. Our research reveals that the frequency spectrum is subject to degradation due to noise, and that aligning features according to temporal and spatial considerations can effectively obtain the lagged similarity. To overcome the limitations of conventional methods, we have: (a) Solved the noise issue by implementing a clean frequency extractor, (b) Upgraded the aligning mechanism to concurrently address both temporal and spatial aspects, and (c) Developed an improved lagged similarity estimator. Our enhanced model, BasicVSR++, achieves significant improvements over the original BasicVSR and leading SR models in the form of video super-resolution benchmarks, ultimately achieving a more efficient framework that achieves comparable results to the more complex models. The code and model are available for download at https://github.com/TheCharn/BasicVSR++.

Large-scale recommender systems face a multitude of challenges, specifically: 
1) user preference patterns across items are scattered and hard to access, 
2) a substantial portion of user-item interaction data is unobserved, 
3) subjective nature of users' preferences makes it difficult to generate accurate predictions.
This research aims to address these challenges by introducing an innovative bicluster-based method that focuses on uncovering user-centric patterns within the interaction data. This approach combines two key techniques - Growing Self-Organizing Maps and Latent Factor Models - to create an adaptive grid that can capture users exhibiting similar preferences within the data across item similarities. When a new query is input, the nearest bicluster containing the user's viewed items is selected to generate predictions based on the distances between the user and the biclusters' characteristics. This method is now available at https://github.com/Chia-Ho/CFCF. Experimental results on various real-world datasets demonstrate its superiority over contemporary methods in predicting user preferences. The proposed approach is shown to significantly reduce subjectiveness in recommendations while leveraging the underlying patterns in the data. This can be seen in the generated recommendation maps and the corresponding performance metrics. Overall, this user-centric method is more efficient than previous techniques, resulting in a higher percentage of accurate recommendations with less computational cost than query times. The underlying theory behind this success is attributed to the bicluster method effectively capturing users with similar preferences and reducing the impact of subjectiveness. This is further validated by the results of the dataset-specific experiments where the model outperformed other state-of-the-art techniques in both overall performance and the percentage of accurate predictions when the user's top-ranked items are considered. Additionally, when the user's preferences are varied, the approach is capable of generating flexible top-N lists with varying levels of accuracy. This is made possible by the user-centric bicluster method that can accommodate users with different preferences in a unified grid, resulting in a higher percentage of accurate predictions across users with both similar and distinct preferences. Lastly, the approach is shown to outperform other state-of-the-art techniques in both overall performance and the percentage of accurate predictions when the user's preferences are varied, demonstrating its potential in real-world recommender systems. The concept of shadows in higher category theory serve as an essential tool, enabling the interpretation of functorial properties through the lens of marks (or targets) in bicategories. Marks have a long-standing presence in the literature, with writers like Berman using the term to describe targets in bicategories as a way to generalize tracker ideas. In this paper, we adopt the notion of targets, with additional requirements, and name them shadows. Critical to our research, we establish that these shadows form alegitimate higher category, consisting of structured marked marked pseudofunctors. By leveraging this category, we can reframe marks as a fundamental component of bicategories equipped with shadows. This refined approach allows us to construct marks from premarks through the application of a homotopy coherent functoriality test, which we identify as a key property of shadows. Ultimately, this refined understanding, incorporating marks derived from shadows, enables us to achieve homotopy invariance for the marks in our study. In support of this, we provide various proofs, accompanied by key properties and marks-related theorems, many of which originate from Berman's work in <arXiv:2012.00642> and fully extended to the realm of shadows. Furthermore, we introduce the concept of factorization chains, establishing that marks factorized into factorization chains are closed under composition. In this context, we also develop the spectral theory of marks, describing the decomposition of marks in relation to factorization chains. Through this research, we provide multiple examples, often constructed by hand, to illustrate diverse marking patterns. In the course of our study, we analyze various higher categorical concepts, effectively testing their applicability to marks in bicategories equipped with shadows. In this context, we proved multiple theorems, establishing the relationship between marks in bicategories equipped with shadows and key higher categorical concepts, notably marking groups and marking homotopy groups. Ultimately, this research is grounded in our understanding of marks in shadows, expressed through the concept of marking groups. In this context, we introduced the concept of strong marking groups, developing the marking group theorem and establishing key properties in marks in shadows. Our method utilizes a two-stage process. Initially, we use a U-Net model to identify areas in images that contain significant image details. Subsequently, we create a style profile by combining the features of these areas from multiple images. Our approach allows for the efficient conversion of under-exposed images to over-exposed images and vice versa while maintaining a natural aesthetic. Our research reveals that the majority of image details are concentrated in areas with intermediate brightness, and our results demonstrate that our method is capable of producing more natural and detailed output compared to the ACES algorithm and the SRN algorithm, particularly in low-light and high-light scenarios. In our study, the accuracy of event reconstruction was evaluated against multiple criteria, including geometric metrics and machine learning features, and we observed that decreasing the size of our compressed data while increasing the number of latent variables results in a notable improvement in reconstruction quality. It's noteworthy that our method encompasses a wide range of event patterns, but it was initially developed with detector systems consisting of many small detectors in mind. Therefore, the proposed approach has immense potential for applications in various sparse three-dimensional data sets. Additionally, the source code used in this study has been made publicly available for other researchers to access at the designated URL. By doing so, we aim to demonstrate that our approach can successfully reduce the dimensionality of real-world particle physics data, thereby proving its feasibility and effectiveness in this domain. Once validated on real-world data, our method can be integrated into the FTD detector system for the International Linear Collider, where it can significantly contribute to the experiment's success. There's also a possibility that our algorithm can be adapted for use in other sparse three-dimensional data sets, such as those encountered in cosmic ray research. A type of convex geometric hypergraph, known as cgh, comprises a set of subsets originating from a collection of convex polygons in the plane that overlap in various combinations. Researchers introduced a concept called the geometricity degree of a hypergraph to gauge the minimum number of edges that need to be removed in order for the remaining edges to form a geometric hypergraph. In our study, we examine the amount of edges needed to be eliminated from a geometric hypergraph in order for the remaining edges to constitute a saturated geometric hypergraph, where all vertices of the original hypergraph are covered. We discovered that this amount can be as low as Ω(n) for geometric hypergraphs, where n represents the number of vertices of the hypergraph. To achieve this result, we first prove that any geometric hypergraph containing at least 2n edges has a subhypergraph with at most 2n edges that includes all the vertices of the original hypergraph. We then demonstrate that this subhypergraph is also geometric by showing the edges of the subhypergraph can be formed by taking subsets of a set of convex polygons that overlap in certain combinations. We also established a lower bound for the geometricity degree by showing that any geometric hypergraph must have at least 4n edges in order for its edges to form a saturated geometric hypergraph. We arrived at this conclusion after finding that any 2n edges of a geometric hypergraph cannot all be contained within one convex polygon without any of the edges intersecting. We also established upper and lower bounds for the geometricity degree based on other geometricity parameters. Additionally, we found that for geometric hypergraphs with certain properties, such as those formed from triangles, the amount of edges needed can be as high as Ω(n^2) and up to O(n^2) edges. We introduce UniToPatho, a large histopathological dataset consisting of 15,376 images and accompanying histological descriptions from the University of Genoa. This dataset serves as a valuable resource for researchers tackling colorectal polyps classification and adenoma grading. Comprising images of hyperplastic polyps, serrated polyps, adenomatous polyps and normal colon tissue, as well as a sub-set labeled as high-risk adenomas, UniToPatho provides essential information for computational pathologists. Its development from conventional histological slides, processed through a standard laboratory approach, mimics real-world clinical settings. Its availability should contribute to the advancement of computer-assisted diagnosis and, by extension, help reduce colorectal cancer mortality rates in Italy. This work extensively evaluates various deep learning architectures for polyp classification, including ResNet, SE-Net, DenseNet and Auto-Encoder based models among others, to determine the most effective approaches. For the abnormality grading task, we explored multiple regression and multi-class classification algorithms with a range of architectures including ResNet, SE-Net, DenseNet and Auto-Encoder. Our experiments show that a combination of Deep Regressor with SE-Net and Pre-Act ResNet outperformed other configurations, achieving 93.44% accuracy in polyp classification and a mean absolute error of 0.14 for adenoma grading. Deep learning-based solutions for synthetic aperture radar (SAR) image processing have gained significant traction recently, primarily because of their capacity to process large images efficiently. Nevertheless, most current deep models overlook the inherent characteristics of RGB pixel values in finalized SAR images, which are generated in the logarithmic domain. To address this, this paper introduces a multi-resolution framework based on a hierarchical generative adversarial network to perform super-resolution tasks on SAR images while maintaining their native image characteristics. The proposed model is evaluated using a large dataset of real, high-resolution SAR images collected from various airborne platforms, along with a companion simulator for generating lower-resolution images based on real scene content. Experimental results confirm that MrSARP outperforms competing state-of-the-art models in an objective comparison. Additionally, MrSARP demonstrates a flexible capacity to handle various super-resolution tasks, including converting log-ratio RGB values to log-ratio or linear RGB values. As a practical example, this paper showcases the implementation of a successful up-sampling technique from $16\times$ using a single model trained on resolution pairs of $16\times 16$ pixels. The companion code and data for this research are available at https://github.com/M-Mohammadi/MrSARP.

Amanuensis leverages cutting-edge AI techniques, in conjunction with advanced handwriting recognition tools, to create a comprehensive solution for businesses and organizations struggling to keep up with paper-based documentation. This report serves as a introductory guide, outlining the design, development, and implementation of Amanuensis. Additionally, we will be demonstrating two complementary approaches: handwritten document retrieval and handwriting-driven information extraction. These innovative approaches not only tackle real-world challenges but also serve as a foundation for further advancements, enabling the development of more sophisticated applications and features.
